Mr. Speaker, this bill is being reintroduced to permanently and legislatively entrench 54-40 as Canada's international land and marine boundary with the United States at the southern tip of the Alaska panhandle, more commonly known as the A-B line.
It is particularly important now because of the hijacking of the MV Fonzie and Viscount this summer and the kidnapping of the crews by the U.S. Coast Guard.

The purpose is to delete the 10-year limitation period for litigation and to provide a fair limitation period for victims of radiation exposure and injury.
Modem medicine now recognizes latency periods of up to 30 years for radiation induced exposure. Surely laws passed by this Parliament must recognize medical realities and the rights of Canadians.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition) moved:
speechtext:
That this House condemns the government for its mismanagement
of the Canadian economy, including:
1)	the threat to impose a new 9 per cent sales tax that is regressive, inequitable, invisible and inflationary;
2)	an unjustifiable high interest rate policy, with an interest rate spread between Canada and the United States that is at record highs;
3)	negligence in the management of Canadian trade causing unparalleled reductions in our trade balance and a loss of jobs, and threatening the survival of many formerly thriving Canadian industries;
4)	abandonment of Canadian primary producers with resulting undermining of the farming, fishing and forest industries; and
5)	continued neglect of regional disparities.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the new 9 per cent sales tax is the ultimate confession of failure of a government which said that it was dedicated to fiscal responsibility.
This government has lost control of the economy. Interest rates are spiralling upward. In five years the total public debt of Canada since Confederation has doubled. Annual deficits are still around $30 billion per year, and all of this despite the largest tax increases during the last five years in the history of our Confederation.

The Conservatives have increased taxes 31 times since 1984. If you add up the tax increases for a single-income family with two children and an annual income of $23,600, which in Canada means you are below the poverty line, the Tories increased their taxes by 60 per cent in the past five years. If you happen to be an average Canadian with an annual income of $45,000, thanks to the Tories your taxes went up 30 per cent in five years. If you are wealthy with an annual income of $100,000, that increase was only 8 per cent and if you earn $200,000 annually, it was only 4 per cent. Everybody knows this
Supply
isn't fair. There is no equity in all this. The same applies to the new sales tax. It isn't fair either.
After letting their expenditures get completely out of control and raising personal income tax levels to the saturation point, Tories are now inflicting on Canadians the biggest, sneakiest and most regressive tax grab in our history. The impact of this tax will be particularly severe on lower and middle-income families. This means that the people in the poorest and most remote regions of our country will suffer most.
How big is this tax, Mr. Speaker? Well, if we add up all personal income tax collected by all ten provinces and the two territories, that amount is still less then what the Tory Government is going to collect from Canadians through its new sales tax. This is a tax that will be paid on practically all goods and services purchased by Canadians: shoes, socks, shirts, skirts, hats and coats, piano lessons, home repairs, plane tickets, stamps, lottery tickets, paper napkins, toothpaste and aspirin. Mr. Speaker, I have only twenty minutes -

The tax does not meet any of the criteria which the Prime Minister of this country and the Minister of Finance set forth for the tax. It does not meet one solitary principle they outlined to Canadians. They have been dishonest about this tax right from the beginning, right from day one.
Hear, hear!

Listen to what they said, Mr. Speaker. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance said that this tax would be revenue neutral. We asked them what this new vocabulary meant. The Minister and the Prime Minister said during the election campaign and prior to that, and I use their words: "Not one penny of additional tax", will be paid as a result of this new sales tax. Those were their words to Canadians during the election campaign. The Minister's own technical paper says there will be $5.5 billion more taken from Canadians.
The Canadian Federation of Independent Business says that that amount is $10 billion more. That is the figure used by the chairman of the finance committee of the House of Commons, the member for Mississauga South, who is in the House. Yet the Minister and Prime Minister said that that member was not right, and yet he

September 28, 1989
Supply
was telling the truth. Now we are faced nationally with a new $29.7 billion tax grab.
Shame.

The Minister and the Prime Minister told Canadians it would be revenue neutral. Saying this tax would be revenue neutral was somewhat like saying that hurricane Hugo was like a warm summer breeze.

And what about the visibility of this tax? The Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance told us that consumers would be well aware of the tax and that it would appear separately on the sales slip, so we would see what proportion it would be of the sale price. The tax was supposed to be visible. And then one day, the Minister woke up in a cold sweat.
He suddenly realized that if his new sales tax appeared separately on the bill, consumers would know what they had to pay as a result of the tax and would know exactly who was responsible for this extra cost.
But the most important thing from his point of view is that if eveiyone knew what the tax rate was, he could not increase it eveiy year as he did with the old manufacturers' tax. The Minister of Finance increased this invisible tax from 9 per cent to 10, 11, 12 per cent, in short by 3.5 per cent in 5 years.

Now the tax will not be visible. It will not be on the sales slip. Instead, the minister is going to give to every business a little sticker to put at the check-out counter. The sticker will say, "Notice: Somewhere in your total bill is the new 9 per cent sales tax. If you cannot afford it, put some of those things back. Have a nice day" signed by Brian Mulroney.
The Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister said they would impose this tax only with provincial co-operation. In 1987 the minister told this House of Commons that without provincial co-operation any such sales tax would be, to use his words, unworkable; not a difficult tax to impose, not harder to do, but unworkable. So what happened? The Conservative government is now imposing a tax on Canadians which they themselves said was
unworkable. It is now being imposed without provincial co-operation.
The Prime Minister and minister said that they would remove the income tax surtaxes. They did not. They said they would lower personal tax rates. They did not.

The Prime Minister and the Minister said that the tax would be easy to administer, but that is not true!
The Canadian Federation of Independent Business believes that applying the tax will be a nightmare, much more complex that the taxes imposed by other countries;
4,000	new tax collectors-additional bureaucrats; a million small and medium-sized businesses will have to collect the tax for the Minister; every small business will have to spend $2,000 more because of the tax; the Retail Council of Canada says that it will cost $2 billion to collect the "easy to administer" tax; it will take more machines, two sets of accounts, two sets of cheques, two sets of transmittal forms. It is total anarchy for every private business person, for every small business in the country!

For example, the homebuilders' association told the finance committee the tax will increase the average house price by $3,000. That is just the average.
What about food? Originally the government said the tax would apply to food. We protested, Canadians protested. We deposited petitions here in the House.
Finally, in response to Canadians everywhere say-ing:"We don't want a tax on food", the Minister of Finance rose in this House on September 2, 1987, two years ago, and as reported at page 8700 of Hansard stated:
Let me make it absolutely clear. There is no proposal in this
document or any other document in Canada to tax food. That is a
fact.
Those were the minister's words. That was not a fact. That was pure fiction; that was pure deception; that was not coming clean with Canadians.
Hear, hear!

In 1987, we thought that the minister had relented. More important, all Canadians thought so too. Almost every newspaper in the country ran headlines that read: "No tax on food, says Minister of Finance". Now, the minister is laughing at Canadians; laughing at this House of Commons. He says that is not what he said. He said he just said there would be no tax on groceries. He said that he was very precise.
He knew exactly what he was doing. He knew that Canadians would assume that he had meant that he was not going to tax food. What did he do when he saw those headlines? He did not say anything to correct them. What did he do during the election? He did not say a word. He left Canadians with the impression that there would be no tax on food and now he says: "It's only basic groceries". He knows full well that if he had told the truth to Canadians he would not still be in his office as Minister of Finance.
Hear, hear!

What is the situation now? All food in restaurants, cafeterias, snack-bars, will be taxed. He is still debating the merits of taxing certain canned and frozen foods, and a whole range of other frozen products. About the only thing Canadians can be thankful for is they will not pay tax on food on trains; they will not get the chance because there will not be any more passenger trains left in the country.

Shame!

The restaurant industry says that the new tax increases their tax burden by 612 per cent. Loblaws warns that food prices could jump by 10 per cent. The minister is proposing a confusing, hodge-podge of rules and regulations which will result in a whole bunch of ridiculous distinctions.
A frozen pizza in a grocery store is not going to be taxed unless it is heated up in the store before you get in. But if you buy a pizza from a pizza parlour, it will be taxed.
The same carton of milk will be taxed if you buy it in a restaurant, but it will not be taxed if you buy it in a grocery store. Milk in a paper cup is taxable in a restaurant, but in a carton it might not be taxed under certain conditions. Under the so-called streamlined accounting procedures milk, might be taxable and tax-free in the same store at different times of the year. That is a shambles, Mr. Speaker. That is ridiculous. How do you expect the corner grocery store, the comer pharmacy to deal with a confusion like this? Mr. Bulloch, in this sense, was right when he called the whole tax a nightmare.
To add insult to injury, the Prime Minister is trying to sell this as a tax cut. He is going across the country and saying: "Look, we are lowering the 13.5 per cent tax to a 9 per cent tax". That is an unbelievably fraudulent way to treat Canadians.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, it does not take a mathematical genius to figure out that a new 9 per cent tax at the retail level on a $300 armchair for your home would come to $27. But the $27 tax at 9 per cent on a $300 armchair is more than the 13.5 per cent tax on the wholesale price of that armchair of $100 which would only be $13.50.
So a retail tax at 9 per cent is higher than a 13.5 per cent tax at the wholesaler distribution level. Anybody can understand that, except the Prime Minister of Canada.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, we see that not a single criterion announced by the Prime Minister and the Finance Minister has been met. Not one! It is not revenue neutral, it is not visible, it is not easy to administer, the provinces are not participating, the personal income tax rate is not lower, the individual

income surtax is not eliminated and it has an inflationary impact.
This tax therefore meets none of the criteria, the principles set even by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance and now they ask us to find alternatives.
There is no alternative to this tax. Get rid of it! Do not impose it. Go back to the drawing board. That is the alternative!
This tax cannot be salvaged or rescued. It does not meet any of the principles which the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance set forth to this House. This tax is nothing but a licence to print money for the government. It is a licence that Canadians want revoked. This tax is coming out of their pockets. It is coming out of our savings accounts, pension cheques, family allowance cheques, unemployment insurance cheques, our budgets for clothes and shoes, and it is on top of rental payments, mortgage payments, and utility bill payments.
As I said to the students at Dalhousie last week and will say again at the University of British Columbia on Monday, for the first time in the history of this country we have a tax on learning, a tax on reading, a tax on literacy, a tax on books. Yet, the Prime Minister, talking to his national convention a few weeks ago, said that education was the priority in the next four years of his government. What a farce! What deception!
It is a tax on pollution-control equipment from a government that said it would do everything to stop pollution. It is a tax on sickness. It is a tax on housing. It is a tax on raising children. It is a tax on the necessities of life. For God's sake, Mr. Speaker, it is even a tax on death.
It is a tax to pay for the government's own mismanagement. It is a tax to pay for the government's own incompetence. We will all pay hundreds and thousands of dollars more for the simple reason that the Tory government has made a complete mess of the fiscal situation. They botched it and now they want Canadians to try to rescue them and pay the price. Well I say, Mr. Speaker, it cannot be rescued. It cannot be tinkered with. It is so fundamentally flawed it has to be scrapped and
the minister has to go back to the drawing board and withdraw the tax.
We intend to fight this tax all the way. It is a bad tax. We are telling this government it is time to scrap this idea and go back to the drawing board. Canadians are fed up with the dishonesty behind the tax. Canadians are fed up with this 9 per cent tax. They are fed up with this government.
I say to the Prime Minister: "You had better listen to what the people of Canada are telling us and your own members." It is coming in loud and clear whether you live in Whitehorse, Vancouver, Toronto, Trois-Rivieres, Halifax or Comer Brook. It is coming from ordinary Canadians, from the elderly, from seniors, from our students, from single mothers, from the business community, and it is virtually unanimous. It is saying to the Prime Minister of this country: "Scrap this tax. No more double talk. No more of these extravagant newspaper ads. No more phoney sales pitches. No more of this tax. Scrap it, get rid of it, and bring us back something that makes sense".
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I think we have just had an impassioned analysis of the situation. I would like to ask the Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra whether in fact, given the parameters of this tax, and given the fact that everything the Prime Minister said he did not do he has done, do you think that the Prime Minister will actually listen to Canadians and listen to the Leader of the Opposition? Do you really think he will scrap this tax?

I think if the Prime
Minister listens to Canadians, if he listens to his own members of Parliament, some of whom are in the Chamber today, if he travels about the country as all of us are travelling listening to our own constituents and Canadians everywhere, he will not only get the message, he will start feeling the heat.
If I were the Minister of Finance I would listen very carefully to the daily pronouncements of his Prime Minister because I think the Prime Minister is wavering.
September 28, 1989

If I were the Minister of Finance I would feel the Bunsen burner right under my backside.

I listened very carefully to the speech of the Leader of the Official Opposition, and I agreed with virtually everything he had to say. I have a question. I heard him say that he was against this sales tax, that this is a mean and a terrible tax, and he had a whole host of good critical comments to make. The question I want to put to him is a very simple one. Does he and his Party oppose the concept of a consumption tax? Would he commit himself and his party today to never, ever supporting a consumption tax of this nature, that they are against the idea of imposing a sales tax on the people of Canada? Perhaps a very tight answer might be appropriate for this question.

Only a government has the authority under our rules to bring in a tax. As you know, we cannot amend it from the floor. It has to have the warrant of the Crown signed by the Minister of Finance in order to make it applicable.
We are examining a tax that does not meet any of the criteria which the government itself put on a tax, criteria which we stated in our minority report in the last parliament were necessary even before you could consider a value added or a consumption tax, or something of that sort. We said it would have to be visible if there were any way we would ever contemplate it; it would have to be provincially drafted and co-ordinated, and it is not; we said there would have to be some progressivity in it. It is so warped on the basis of the minister and the Prime Minister's own criteria that there is no way, in our view, that it can be improved, or amended. You have to go right back to the drawing board.
We said during the election that we were against the sales tax. We still are. We would look at a better combination of progressivity, at a better balance between taxes on the various elements in an economy than this.
Also, it has to be looked at within the general scope of the economy. Fiscal and monetary policy have to be taken together. Also, consideration must be given to what the government has allowed to happen to our
Supply
exchange rate as part of the secret deal that I believe exists with the United States under the trade agreement.

I appreciated the response given by the Leader of the Official Opposition. I have been trying to think, while he was making his very thoughtful presentation today, how we differ in terms of the Liberal Party and the New Democratic Party. I think I have found the way.
We are clearly of a mind that we oppose the principle and concept of a national sales tax, of a consumption tax, of a tax on consumption of any kind. We totally oppose it. I think what I am hearing the Hon. Leader of the Official Opposition say is that, on principle, they do not necessarily oppose that, but they oppose this particular tax. This is a mean, rotten, bad tax, there is no question about it. But perhaps in another form, in another way, they would consider it.
If we are trying to figure out how we do differ, because we are both fighting this tax, would he agree that perhaps this is the way that we do differ? We oppose it on principle and you really buy the principle, it is just that you really oppose this particular tax?

I want to suggest to the Hon. Member for Kamloops, who in an earlier incarnation shared a lot of our views, that he can read what he wants into what I have said, but should not put too much confidence in his reading.
The real difference between a Liberal approach to taxation and an NDP approach to taxation is that someday we will have to implement it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: I would like to ask the hon. member, since he sees that this tax is such a negative tax and such a blight, according to what he has had to say, what concrete and positive proposals he would like to bring to the Canadian people as an alternative to this tax?

The hon. member is entitled, representing a constituency in this country, to put that question. Before I answer it fully, she really should assure me that what she reflects carries the support of all the people in her constituency. We heard her colleague from Edmonton deposit about 6,000 names representing what his constituency feels. I wonder whether she could assure us that she speaks for her constituency and that the people are behind that tax as she seems to indicate she is.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened very carefully to the speech by the Hon. Leader of the Opposition. Since I am getting on in years, I have discovered that much of what is too exaggerated does not exist. I feel that to be so negative on so many points indicates a certain weakness in the argument.
What he has convinced me of is that we are not doing this because we intend to win a popularity contest. We are doing it because this government has a long-term plan to build a strong economy for Canada. The plan is aimed at such vital objectives as reducing our deficit, controlling the growth of national debt, of removing obstacles to Canada's economic growth, and fostering innovation and competitiveness in the business sector.
Our plan is working. There are factual independent measurements of its progress because 1.5 million new jobs have been created in Canada over the past five years; 86 per cent of them full-time, and 57 per cent filled by women. Unemployment rates have dropped in
every region of our country. Youth unemployment has dropped by 7 per cent as more and more Canadians have joined in our economic renewal. The economy has expanded by 20 per cent. Business investment is up by 95 per cent, and average after tax disposable income is up by $1,600. The government's annual deficit has been cut by about $9.5 billion below its level of 1984-1985.
Our plan is also aimed at providing more assistance to Canadians in need through our social programs. That is something the opposition always seems to forget. Only by having a dynamic economy, led by a vibrant business sector, coupled with a fair and effective tax structure, can we provide these services today without imposing an insupportable burden of debt on future generations.
I have listened carefully to the comments made by opposition members about our comprehensive proposals for sales tax reform, and frankly, I am not very impressed. I am waiting to hear their proposals for sales tax reform. How could they replace the current manufacturers sales tax, a tax that has been universally condemned by nearly every interest group in this country as a destructive, discriminatory, and unfair tax?
This important reform of our tax system is an essential element of the plan for economic renewal that this government began five years ago.

As far as interest rates are concerned, I maintain that it would be irresponsible and in fact counter-productive to lower rates before inflationary symptoms have eased off. It would certainly not be a good way to manage the economy. There would be a heavy price to pay for any short-term relief that might result. Business, labour and other levels of government must realize that this Government will not tolerate measures that are inflationary. However, to beat inflation, both the public and private sectors of our economy must be involved.
The federal Government will continue to implement responsible monetary and financial policies in order to defuse inflationary trends. As inflation eases off, we will see the benefits as reflected by a drop in interest rates, a more competitive economy, stronger growth, more jobs and a higher standard of living for all Canadians.



Our GST package, and I stress "package", contributes to these objectives. First, by contributing to the deficit reduction effort and ensuring that we can continue to pay for programs and services Canadians value. Second, by helping to ensure that Canada can compete in the world economy. Third, by improving the over-all fairness of the tax system.
Since we released our proposals in August, a number of misconceptions about the GST have arisen. I welcome this opportunity today to put these misconceptions to rest and to get the facts on the table.
To begin with, it can be taken as a given that we would all prefer taxes to be lower rather than higher. That goes without saying. But it also goes without saying that they are a necessary part of a civilized and modern society. The government knew that its proposals would be controversial.
No one likes taxes and we recognize the sacrifices that Canadians have been asked to make to help deal with the deficit. Life could have been easier for all of us if we had been content to let the subject of tax reform drift, as past governments have done. But, for a government that takes its responsibility seriously, that was just not acceptable. Our objective is to have the fairest and most efficient tax system that can be designed.
Very few Canadians are aware that they already pay a hidden federal sales tax of 13.5 per cent when they purchase manufactured goods. They do not realize that this 13.5 per cent manufacturer's tax generates production losses of as much as $9 billion annually for Canadian businesses, exporters and workers.
The present tax has another drawback: widely varying rates increase the risk of distorting consumer choices.
If prices contain distortions, it is practically impossible to make an informed choice. Our economy's resources are not being used to their fullest extent. We cannot maximize our production potential and that has an impact on jobs.

The existing tax is very complex. It applies to only 75,000 businesses but has generated 22,000 special provisions and administrative interpretations.
Under the existing federal tax, which may be as high as 19 per cent on certain goods, we are taxing business inputs while our foreign competitors do not. Our entrepreneurs are therefore at a disadvantage, both domestically and on foreign markets, and this has an impact on employment.
Furthermore, with the exception of automobiles where the tax affects wholesalers, the taxable value of imported goods does not include the foreign manufacturer's marketing and distribution costs, while these are usually included in the value of domestic goods.
This means that on average, the amount of tax paid on most Canadian goods is almost a third more than the tax collected on imports. The importer pays a lower tax and can therefore sell more cheaply. This, too, costs jobs.
The federal sales tax as we know it today goes back 65 years, to a time when production and distribution patterns were relatively simple. However, the economy has changed drastically since then, and Canadians must move ahead.
Sixty-five years ago, manufacturers manufactured and distributors distributed, with little involvement in retail sales. Today, the situation has changed. Many retailers are involved in manufacturing, and some manufacturers are directly involved in retail sales. Other industrialized countries are in the same situation and have adapted their tax system. Today, only Canada has maintained a tax on manufactured goods.

I think it is safe to say that the GST is not a well kept secret and that by January 1991 we will make sure that consumers are well aware of how much GST they are paying. Certainly GST is going to be much more visible than the present federal sales tax that is buried throughout the production process. The GST is part of the five-year fiscal plan put forward in the April budget which will see the government's cash requirement reduced year by year to zero. The GST has been designed as an integral part of our fiscal strategy.
I would like to remind the hon. members that the GST is a carefully balanced package. In order to change one element other parts must be balanced. If the rate were to

be lowered another element would have to change. The base would have to broaden, the credit lowered or the deficit increased.
Canadians know by now that our government is serious about revitalizing the Canadian economy and ensuring a strong and prosperous future for this country.
Our record since 1984 speaks for itself. Our critics do not have a monopoly on compassion and fairness when it comes to dealing with Canadians who need assistance. Our government is committed to reforming the tax system to ensure fairness for Canadians right across the country.
We are serious about reducing the cost to government and about reducing the deficit. At the same time we are serious about maintaining the services that Canadians look to their government to provide. The goods and service tax will ensure that these goals are met.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister who was a journalist at the newspaper where I was a cartoonist when I was a university student. I congratulate him for being the Minister responsible, but I have this question that I want to ask him. I am still thinking about the time when I was a student and the Minister was encouraging students. Does the Minister propose taxing cartoons? Does the Minister propose taxing comic strips? Does the Minister propose taxing comic books intended to help educate young people? Does the Minister propose taxing school texts? Is the Minister for students and young people? The Minister said that we had to talk about being fair, I heard him mention the words fair and civilized, and that Canadians have to keep up with progress. Mr. Speaker, is beating up on youth and students progress?

Mr. Speaker, I believe that my hon. colleague is raising an extremely important question. When this tax, this reform project based on a multi-stage tax, was considered, we paid a great deal of attention to fairness. That is why instead of making the choices for the citizens ourselves, we ensured that they would make the choices themselves and those who have less freedom of choice because they have less income, in particular students, would receive compensating credits.
As for books, you must understand as well that we granted special provisions for universities, libraries and public agencies. This is not a tax on culture, if you will. To be fair and equitable, for the rate to be low, the tax must apply to as many items as possible. Otherwise, it is taking from one pocket and putting in another. But to restore fairness to a system, I agree with him that without credits and compensating measures, it would be an unfair, regressive system. We have what has been described by the taxation office as perhaps the fairest system in the world, according to tax experts' studies.

Mr. Speaker, I listened to the hon.
minister very carefully. He is a man of honour and I have a great deal of respect for him. I have had dealings with him in the past and I have some respect for him.
I find it rather strange, because when a goods and services tax was first announced by the government Canadians were told that it would be revenue neutral. They were told that it would be visible. They were told that it would be simple. They were told that it would be integrated with the provincial scheme.
We did not hear at that time about this tax being used to reduce deficits. We were not being told that this was going to be used to reduce a national debt. We were not told that this would involve some 6,000 bureaucrats which has got to be an anathema to any true Conservative.
Canadians are getting a little bit cheesed off with the lying that is going on; they do not like to be lied to. This government promised that it was going to be revenue neutral, and now we are hearing that once this cash cow gets into the barn the government is going to run off into the stable and pull a few billion dollars off this cow every time it needs it to reduce the deficit or the national debt.
Why? The question is: "Why has this government lied to Canadians and why does it continue to lie to Canadians?" That is the question, Mr. Speaker.

I thank the hon. member for Nickel Belt for his question and his remarks. I would tell him that we did not lie. We have explained from the beginning that the purpose of this type of mechanism of tax reform would not be used per se to increase the revenue of the government. We said it would be used to replace a bad

tax, the present federal sales tax, and to make it, I would say, not regressive.
I think the hon. member would agree with me that we have devised a system of credit because we have also promised that it would not hinder affordability of housing. So the package in itself is a very well balanced package and it does not in any way bring additional revenue to the government for other spending.
As far as visibility is concerned, I would be inclined to smile at this because the tax does not exist and it is probably the most visible thing in the country at the present time and will remain so, as it is in other countries, for the future.
As far as a national tax with the provinces is concerned, for two years we have worked with the provinces to try to arrive at a system, which we would have preferred. We know that to implement such a tax is a difficult political thing to do, even if it is necessary. To get 11 governments to come together at the one precise time is not an easy objective to reach. We have tried to do it but we can understand and respect the other governments of the provinces that do not have the problem we have with their sales tax, which is a rather straightforward consumption tax. It works. In our case we have a disastrous tax.
He talks about revenue and deficit reduction. We know that the present sales tax is extremely porous. While we increase the rate the income keeps going down proportionately because manufacturers will find ways of escaping and avoiding the tax. Through the new system, which is much more modern and which has been chosen by all modem countries, we will prevent our revenue from disappearing and in this way we will help reduce the deficit.

Mr. Speaker, in asking my question I want to make it very clear that I oppose the tax and think it should be knocked out completely, not tinkered with. But the government and the finance committee have indicated on a number of occasions that they are prepared to do some tinkering with the tax. If that is as close as they can come to listening to the people of Canada and will go ahead with that tinkering, while I reject that idea I will ask a question of the minister who on other

occasions has indicated a great knowledge of the credit union system in Canada.
The credit unions have said that they would be disproportionately taxed by the new goods and services tax. In their submission before the finance committee they talked about financial services being exempt. However, when the GST goes into effect credit unions will have to pay the tax on shared networks, training, consulting, tax processing, and cheque clearing because of the way their system is set up. Can this minister inform us in the House if plans are under way to continue to tinker with this tax to change it to apply to the credit unions?

I would like to thank the hon. member for a very important question. Indeed the problem he has indicated to me is a serious and difficult one. I would like to inform him officially today that we are aware of the particular situation facing the co-operatives and credit unions and that we are going to find a way of solving that problem because we do not want to be unfair to this movement.

Mr. Speaker, I must say that I am absolutely delighted to participate in the debate today and pleased to have an opportunity to lend some commentary toward the motion that simply describes the host of ways in which this government has mismanaged the Canadian economy and, as my colleague from Nickel Belt said earlier today, how we have been exposed to a whole set of lies by the government. I suppose we might as well call a spade a spade and simply call it that.
When you look at even a small part of Canada-and I refer simply to the constituency that I have the honour to represent, the Kamloops constituency-we have had again a whole host of mistruths stated regarding what this government would do for our area. For example, it suggested that it would enhance VIA Rail service. Now we find out that it is going either to eliminate totally VIA Rail service in some parts of Canada or curtail it very seriously.
Then it said it was going to support more post-secondary education. Yet before us on the Order Paper there will soon be legislation to cut back on transfer payments to the provinces for post-secondary education.
It said it was interested in helping develop our forest resources, yet the government refuses to sign the forest agreements with the province of British Columbia to add funding for reforestation, silviculture. It simply suggests

that we go to the Western Diversification Fund. We are not talking about diversification of the economy; we are simply talking about enhancing the forest resource.
It suggested that it would help the mining industry. Rather than helping the mining industry it is eliminating programs that encourage the exploration for more and new mineral deposits.
It said that it was concerned about illiteracy and we saw that it brought in a tax on reading. I think we are now the only country in the world where the government has imposed a tax on books, periodicals, magazines and reading material to make it more expensive and therefore a disincentive, if you like, to encourage people to develop their reading and analytic skills.
The government said it would help ranchers because of the severe drought situation. There are huge cattle ranches in the central interior that receive no drought assistance and support at all.
It said it would enhance tourism and yet refuses to sign a new tourism agreement with the province of British Columbia. As the tourist association told the finance committee last night, about 30,000 jobs will be lost in this sector because of the 9 per cent sales tax that will be introduced on all tourist services, which will essentially price a good number of our tourist operations out of the market.
It said it would clean up the environment, yet refuses to help any of the municipalities and towns across Canada develop their sewage treatment facilities in terms of a cost sharing basis with the provincial governments which are quite anxious to participate. It promised a comprehensive child care program and then reneged on that child care program; it has abandoned all intentions of supporting that.
It said it would enhance the fishing industry, and we have found out in the last number of days that the fishing industries on the east coast and the west coast are in a state of crisis, a state of collapse, because of the policies of the government.
I could go on and on. The Prime Minister has heard this list before and simply has to stand there and agree that "yes, this is the case; that in spite of all of these promises that we are going to take all of these different
initiatives, we have reneged on them all. We have broken the promises that we have made. We have lied time and time again and that is just the way the world is."
I will tell you, Mr. Speaker, Canadians are fed up with that Tory world and when they get another chance to go to the ballot boxes, once again this will ensure that this set of promises will never even be listened to again in terms of a future government of this country.
I want to, before I get into an analysis of the 9 per cent sales tax, simply refer very briefly to the free trade agreement. While the government was jamming this legislation through the House of Commons it indicated that all sorts of economic opportunities would take place in Canada. Everybody else who had analysed the free trade agreement clearly found once that border was removed, the industrial sector and business sector of Canada would move their operations to the United States where they could produce their materials more cheaply for a whole host of reasons.
Now we have, of course, a very long list of companies that have done just that and have taken advantage of the ease of moving their operations to the United States.
I just want to read a handful of these into the record as an example of this particular transfer of jobs south or, as others call it, the Americanization of Canada: Canron Incorporated shifted production to its plant in Columbia, South Carolina. Burlington Canada Incorporated moved its plants into Georgia and Virginia. Hartz Canada moved its production to a number of United States plants in the deep south. Picker International Canada Incorporated transferred its production to Cleveland, Ohio. International Playing Card Company moved its production to Cincinnati, Ohio. Star Suspension Industries moved its product development to the United States parent plant.
Woodbridge Group moved down to Mexico, again to take advantage of free trade areas on the Mexican-U.S. border. Bendix Safety Restraints moved its plants to Alabama and to the Mexico zone. Marr's Leisure Products moved its production to Newberry, South Carolina. Takahashi Industries moved its production to Seattle, Washington. Executive Dental Supply moved its production to Pullman, Washington. ITW Shakeproof moved

production to Tennessee. Advanced Gibson Canada moved down to Pennsylvania; and Progress Company moved its plant to Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.
K. T. Industries downsized and moved its production facilities to Fort Wayne, Indiana. Northern Telecom, with hundreds of jobs to a total of 1,500, shifted its facilities into Dallas, Texas and down into the southern part of California. United Maple Products moved its production to Vermount. Canadian Coleman moved down to Texas and Kansas. Leviton Manufacturing transferred its production line of electrical goods to the United States, again down into the Mississippi area. I could go on and on, Mr. Speaker.
I just repeat that we now have literally dozens and dozens of major Canadians firms that have moved their production into the United States. There has been the transfer of over 50,000 Canadian jobs into the United States as a result of the free trade deal. We are seeing our worst fears being realized.
However, I want to turn my comments today to the 9 per cent national sales tax, the goods and services tax, or the grief and suffering tax that has become more associated with the title.
I looked at the newspapers this morning that were referring to this tax, as different groups have commented in the last two or three days. Some of the names they used to describe the tax were: a very bad tax, an insidious tax, an oppressive tax, a ridiculous tax, a regressive tax, a vicious tax, a mean tax, a cruel tax, a harsh tax, a punitive tax, a brutal tax, a destructive tax.
I have been looking in newspapers now for the last three weeks at virtually every article and I have yet to find a single group, a single organization, a single agency, a single person with credibility in the tax area that supports this tax and says this is a good idea. The only exception is the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance.
Tsee the hon. member from Edmonton here. I even hear a whole host of Conservative back-benchers say that this is a terrible tax, that they should not be introducing it and that the Minister of Finance should not be pursuing it at this point. Every Premier across

Canada and every single group that has spoken out in the last couple of weeks have spoken against this tax.
Even the Liberal party has spoken against this tax. I think it is appropriate to make the comment that what the Liberal party is saying is that it does not support this 9 per cent tax. It might support a 7 per cent tax or a 6 per cent tax with some modification and so on.
Oh, oh!

My hon. friends can ask me some questions to elaborate on this at the end of my speech, but it appears to me that the Conservatives think this is a deliriously wonderful 9 per cent cruel, mean tax that they want to impose on the people of Canada. The Liberals are not quite sure that this is the kind of mean, cruel tax that they would impose, but they would modify it somewhat and make their imposition.
I will say that there is one party that will never impose a sales tax, a consumption tax on the people of Canada, and that is the New Democratic Party, never.
Let me continue with what this tax does, this mean, cruel, horrible tax.
It is a crushing tax.

A crushing tax, as my hon. friend indicated. When he says "crushing", he means crushing. This is going to crush the life right out of the economy. It is going to crush the kind of lifestyles that people have been struggling to develop over the last little while.
A typical Canadian family today is going to have not $100, not $200, not $500, but $850 yanked out of its pocket every year as a result of this tax. T hat is the most modest estimate. I have all sorts of information here.
For example, the Consumer's Association of Canada, which has a very through research branch, says that every man, woman and child will be hit with at least $1,000 a year in additional taxes as a result of this 9 per cent tax. That is not the New Democratic Party saying that; it is the Consumer's Association of Canada that says $1,000 a year, at least, for every man, for every woman, for every child. For a typical family of four it is $4,000 minimum that will be yanked out of its pocket.
Not only will those people not have that money to purchase necessary goods and services, but the community will not have that money. In a community like Kamloops with a population of 65,000 people, at $1,000 a

Supply
person hundreds of thousands of dollars each day will be yanked out of that community, dragged down to Ottawa to be spent on some pretty peculiar and questionable uses.
That is not the way you generate economic activity, by taking away that money that could be used to purchase goods and services, certainly those necessary goods and services. What is going to be taxed? From the crib to the coffin, from haircuts to movies, from laundries to lawyers, from kids' snowsuits to hunting licences. These are all new areas that have never been taxed before.
This is the largest tax grab in Canadian history since the imposition of the personal income tax which the government of the day said would last just a couple of years. Back in 1917 the government said that this was a tax to get us out of debt as a result of the war effort and that as soon as we are out of debt it would take away this personal sales tax. We know that personal sales tax has stayed in place and has gone up until now when we have this crushing burden of tax including personal tax, excise tax, and gas tax. Now we are going to add another big tax on our back. This is a party of tax, tax, tax. The Conservative Party is a tax party.
The Minister of Finance will know that since this government came to office in 1984 the average family in Canada has paid at least $1,300 more in federal taxes, and now we are just going to be slammed between the eyes with another 9 per cent consumption tax on all these goods and services.
Nobody can imagine a government that says: "We have got a great idea. We are going to tax snowsuits for children. We are going to tax children's books". Imagine taxing children's books.
Imagine taxing haircuts. My dad is 86 years old. When he goes down to get a haircut with his pension he is going to have to pay a Mulroney sales tax of 9 per cent on his haircut; when he buys his shirts and when he goes to a movie-on everything. This is a cash cow that this government has created to generate, not millions, not thousands of millions, but billions and billions of dollars in additional funds every year.
The economy cannot take it and Canadians will not take it. That is why we say that this government has to back off on this tax initiative. It is not only the New Democratic Party that says this is a tax that we must not
proceed with. There are some other groups that you would be interested in hearing from, Mr. Speaker. The Canadian Federation of Independent Business opposes this tax. The Canadian Organization of Small Business opposes this tax. The Consumer's Association of Canada opposes this tax. The National Council of Welfare opposes the tax. The Canadian Home Builder's Association opposes this tax, because it says that this tax will add thousands of dollars to the price of a new home.
We already know that the housing market is overpriced now and that it is virtually impossible for young Canadians to even consider owning their own home. This government's solution is to tax it again, raise the tax on the price of a new home. But it says: "Well, we are going to exempt rental". That is only partially true because all of the inputs into rental housing, the janitorial services, repairs, renovations, heating, advertising fees, landscaping and maintenance will all be taxed and one can rest assured that the landlord will take those additional 9 per cent taxes and pass them along in terms of the rent. Indirectly, even rentals will be increased substantially as a result of this tax.
That is not all. Wood Gundy, one of the most outstanding financial analysts in the country, has said this is a punitive, mean-spirited tax. The Coalition of Senior Citizens opposes the tax. The One Voice Seniors Network strongly opposes the tax. The Canadian Conference of the Arts strongly opposes the tax. The Canadian Association of Universities opposes the tax. The Canadian Bar Association opposes the tax.
The Canadian food industry is deliriously in opposition to taxation when the pizza at Pizza Hut will be taxed 9 per cent and the pizza you buy in the grocery store will not be taxed. What kind of nonsense is this? What kind of an unfair, biased, discriminatory tax is this? Not surprisingly, the industry opposes it. The Conference Board of Canada opposes it.
I think if we were to honestly analyse the process, we would say that the Conference Board of Canada, with its first-rate research department, looks carefully at these kinds of initiatives and then makes its observations. It came out strongly in opposition to this tax saying that it is going to cost thousands and thousands of jobs. The Conference Board of Canada said that this 9 per cent tax

will lose tens of thousands of jobs in this country. We have to listen to this group.
I do not understand the government. When it is confronted with the Canadian Bankers Association, its friends in the banking community, the Institute for Policy Analysis and its own back-benchers, to whom does it listen? To whom is the Minister of Finance listening? I have yet to hear a single group stand up and say it thinks this tax is a good tax.
Why are people not to trust this Minister of Finance? He said at the beginning of this process that the tax would be revenue neutral, that as we phase out the manufacturers' sales tax, we are going to impose a sales tax but we are not going to make any money out of it. That is not true. Already, this is billions over what the manufacturers' tax brings in. It is billions and billions of dollars over being revenue neutral.
The Minister promised that the tax would be simple. We are seeing quite the contrary. I have here the brief of the members of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business who again are almost unable to speak when they refer to this tax. John Bulloch, one of the most outstanding supporters of the government on almost every issue, says that this government must fall, that the Minister of Finance must resign, and that they ought to be hanging their heads in shame as they back off on this tax and start over with a fair system. He points out on behalf of the small business community that this tax is unworkable, that it cannot be done and is going to be punitive to small business. Small business is all tangled up in red tape now and they have tax collectors hassling them day and night. What will this do? We will have to hire not one, not two, not five, but maybe 10,000 more tax collectors.
New Zealand, with a population of 3.3 million, has over 5,000 new tax collectors. We have a population of 26 million, so when that is factored out, we can say we are going to have thousands more tax collectors now.
I do not know why my friends in the Conservative benches are not up in their seats shouting and yelling today because the small businesses in their communities are going to be harassed beyond belief with new paper flows. There will be a blizzard of forms coming into those businesses and tax collectors will be hassling them. Mr. Bulloch says it is going to cost at least $2 billion for just the small business sectors to comply with this tax.

The Minister of Finance said that he would not proceed with the tax unless the provincial governments co-operated and we would have a melded provincial-federal tax. That has gone by the board completely. Now we are going to have a combined federal-provincial tax in British Columbia of 15 per cent. In Newfoundland it will be 21 per cent and it will be changing right across the whole country. What a mishmash. Not a country in the world has a tax system of that nature.
The minister promised that the tax would be visible on all sales slips. We all know that they have abandoned that promise a long time ago. It will not be visible.
There is so much more one could say and should say. The New Democratic Party not only opposes this tax but opposes the principle of this tax. This is a regressive tax. When a poor family buys snow tires for the winter coming up and has to pay a 9 per cent sales tax and the wealthy family with an income of $200,000 a year buys those same snow tires, they both pay the same amount of sales tax. How is that fair? How is that just? How is that equitable? That just points out the discriminatory, biased nature of this tax to the middle-income and low-income families of the country.
We as New Democrats oppose this 9 per cent tax. We do not care if the government reduces it to 8 per cent, 6 per cent or 5 five per cent, because we know very well that within a matter of time, it will be jacked up to 10 per cent, 15 per cent, 20 per cent. Some European countries now have it has high as 22 per cent.
In closing, we oppose not only this tax initiative, but we oppose the principle of a consumption tax as being regressive, mean and unfair. We will do everything that we possibly can in the intervening period to convince the government, along with many of the Conservative backbenchers, to stop progressing with this particular tax, to go back to the drawing board and to start over with real tax reform that is fair and ask those corporations and those individuals who are not paying their fair share to start paying their fair share.

I have a very simple question for the hon. member. He says that he and his Party oppose categorically any consumption tax. I would like to ask him whether he supports and agrees with the existing federal manufacturers' sales tax. As a former businessman and as a former manufacturer, I know from experience that the existing manufacturers' sales tax is a major obstacle for Canadian manufacturers and producers in terms of

Supply
fairness, competitiveness and international trade opportunities.
Obviously, the reason for this government's move in proposing a fairer system, which we believe the GST is all about, is to give Canadian producers and manufacturers an opportunity to be competitive both domestically and more importantly, internationally so as to compete on a level playing field which they are not doing today.
The hon. member knows full well that 48 countries around the world have a similar tax to the GST, a value-added or consumption tax, therefore giving an advantage to all of those manufacturers in those countries over our manufacturers in our country. Unless we remove this obstacle, we will not create the opportunities for our manufacturers and producers to create the type of competitive spirit that is held elsewhere around the world and therefore to create the jobs that are necessary to be created.
Does the hon. member support that existing tax? If he does not, what would he and the New Democratic Party replace that tax with? That tax, as he well knows, brings in revenue of some $18 billion today which goes toward many of the social programs as well as many of the things that both my hon. friend and I believe Canadians want, desire, need and will continue to have.
I would like the hon. member to say what he and his party would propose to replace the existing manufacturers' sales tax, if in fact he is opposed to that sales tax and agrees with me that it is an obstacle in the way of Canadian producers and manufacturers.

I appreciate the question of my hon. friend. Yes, indeed, the manufacturers' sales tax has to go. The Minister of Finance on occasion has referred to the existing manufacturers' sales tax as a killer of jobs. I think he used that term, Mr. Speaker. You remember that he said it was a killer of jobs. Yet I am puzzled because if this is a tax that kills jobs, why would the government increase it time and time again? I remember back in 1984 when the Conservative government took office, it was 9 per cent. Now it is 13.5 per cent and I am curious why a government that identifies a tax as a killer of jobs, that creates an unfair advantage for foreign
importers against our own manufacturers, would increase that tax once, twice, three or four times. I am not referring to the hon. member, but the government itself. It is a bit hypocritical to be saying that this is a killer of jobs and then to keep increasing the tax so it can kill off more jobs.
To answer my hon. friend seriously, yes, we believe that the manufacturers' sales tax should be phased out over time. I do not think we have to drop it from 13.5 per cent to zero overnight, but there should be a commitment to phase it out over a period of time that would make sense to the manufacturing community and we should replace it with some changes to our tax system.
Let me offer three or four examples. The United States has in place a minimum corporate tax .The Reagan administration back in 1986 saw all of these corporations that paid no income tax and said that was wrong and that they should pay some, so it introduced a minimum corporate tax. We say we should do that in Canada. As we all well know, there are 60,000 profitable corporations in this country that do not pay a penny in income tax, let alone 50 cents. Let us have the minimum corporate tax to generate some new revenue like they have done in most other countries.
Second may I humbly suggest that many of the corporate tax incentives, the tax exemptions, or the tax loopholes, are not necessary. Billions and billions and billions of dollars each year are lost from our federal treasury through silly corporate tax loopholes. Even the corporations say they are silly and that we do not get the bang for the buck. It costs us $500 million for a certain tax incentive and we do not get very much in return. Let us close off some of these large corporate loopholes.
Name one.

The finance committee has gone on at some length to name some of the silly corporate loopholes. I would ask my friend to name one that works, one that is good. I remember my hon. friends from Alberta who ranted on about all the grants and the freebies in the tax system for the oil companies to explore, while the taxpayers were paying 100 per cent. They moved off on
September 28, 1989

some of those, sensibly. There are many more corporate tax exemptions that ought not to be in existence.
Let me offer my friend one other suggestion. Why is it that our interest rates have to be so high? Why is it that our deficit and debt are jacked up every year because of our increased interest rates? It is Conservative interest rate policy, but it perplexes me that our rates have to be three or four percentage points higher than those in the United States. If we were to drop our interest rates just 2 per cent, we would cut from the deficit over $3 billion just like that.
I could go on to make some suggestions, but a minimum corporate tax is one suggestion, eliminating some of the corporate tax incentive programs is another, lowering interest rates is another suggestion, a more progressive income tax system in the personal side is another. Just as a starter, this indicates that there are many alternatives to increasing revenue through the tax system as opposed to simply imposing a punitive 9 per cent sales tax.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a couple of remarks. The Hon. Member for Kamloops referred to the mismanagement of the economy. I would like to recall that very recently, the World Economic Forum and the International Institute for Management Development indicated a significant improvement in Canada's international competitive position, with our ranking among the 23 major industrialized economies climbing to fourth position this year from sixth in 1987. For mismanagement, this is good management, I would say.
The hon. member referred briefly to the free trade agreement. Whenever we do something that more less looks like what the Americans have done, we are accused of imitating them. We are doing something that the Americans have not done. We are using a different system of taxation. This is something important. It is a modern way of doing it and we are doing it in way which is more generous.
The Hon. Member talked about his father. We were concerned about his father before he made his speech. We want to protect all the fathers of Canada by devising the most progressive credit system and package. This is
Supply
to protect the people who need to be protected, to remove the regressive aspect which exists in the sales tax.
We have made this effort and I think you have to take into account the whole package and not only say we will be taxing everything. We will make sure that people are well protected because if we project the numbers you have given, with so many Canadians paying so much more, we would not have any deficit left next year. I would not mind that, but I do not think this is the way the world would unfold.

That, notwithstanding any standing order of this House, that after

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

I think it is a good opportunity to explore various ways of including more members in these important debates.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have no problem with the motion as proposed by the Official Opposition. The only concern I would have is that the rotation would follow the normal party rotation.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It would follow the normal party rotation on allotted days which is not the same, if there is such a thing as a rotation in this House, as it is on normal second reading.
The House has heard the terms of the motion proposed by the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier. Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the motion?
Agreed.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure today to rise on behalf of the constituents of Kenora-Rainy River and Canadians generally to explain what this particular government has done to our economy since its election in 1984 and its re-election in 1988.
This government has a record of mismanaging the economy in just a very few short years that is unprecedented in the history of this great nation of ours. This government's record, for lack of a better word, is tainted. Canadians have lost all confidence in the government's capability to manage the affairs of this country.
When the Conservatives took power in 1984-and we go back to this over and over again-Canada's national debt stood at $170 billion. Today our national debt stands at $340 billion. For members opposite who might have a hard time understanding this, that means that the national debt has doubled since 1984.
At a time when everyone has been asked to tighten their belts, the government has increased its expenditures. Where is the leadership in this? How can Canadians be expected to carry the burden of deficit reduction when their own government spends and spends and spends?
The Minister of Finance claims that his goods and services tax proposal is the be all and end all of tax reform. There are so many problems with this particular GST that it seems to me that the government's only alternative, and we say this very honestly, would be to scrap it and go back to the drawing board. The goods and services tax is nothing but a tax grab.
Canadians are fed up with tax increases. They are fed up with the burden imposed on them time and time again. Since this government took power, Canadians have seen tax increases no fewer than 30 times. I can
only say what Canadians have been saying in the press lately, "Don't you think enough is enough?"
Not only will the goods and services tax increase taxes. It is inflationary, and I believe higher interest rates will be the end result. The hidden nature of the goods and services tax means that Canadians will not know how much tax they are paying.
This government has promised that the GST would be visible. Well, as we have seen on numerous occasions, it is just another one of those broken promises. Canadians no longer trust anything this government says. As for integrity, the record speaks for itself.
To keep the GST hidden from Canadians is despicable. The government is telling Canadians, "Trust us." There is no trust in this government and there is no integrity in this government.
In the budget tabled earlier this year, the government chose to tax back seniors' pensions and family allowances. The Finance Minister said that everyone had to chip in and help reduce the deficit. Reducing the deficit on the backs of seniors and those less fortunate is ridiculous.
The Finance Minister said that he was not tampering with the universality of social programs. However, the Finance Committee chairman admitted in an interview with The Ottawa Citizen on Saturday, September 23, that the government's real agenda is to do away with universal social programs.
It is unbelievable that on one side they can say that it is not and on the other side they say that it is. It is really difficult to understand who is telling the truth in this regard. Coupled with the goods and services tax, the claw-back provision of old age security pensions and family allowances, means that seniors will have lost what little buying power they have left. Every purchase made will now be made more difficult. Their budgets, which are already stretched to the limit, will be considerably affected by the goods and services tax.
At a time in their lives when they should be enjoying their retirement years, seniors will now be faced with difficult financial decisions and increased burdens. Where is the fairness this government claims to profess? There is no fairness. This government could not care less about being fair.

The goods and services tax will severely restrict small businesses in northwestern Ontario that depend heavily on tourism. Increased administrative costs, increased taxes and the higher prices for services will kill this very volatile industry in my region. My riding sits on the Canada-U.S. border. Communities such as Rainy River, Emo, Stratton and Fort Frances depend on tourist dollars from the United States. Businesses located in these communities are already struggling to survive as people cross over to the U.S. to buy gas and grocery items. The goods and services tax will serve only to encourage my constituents to cross over to the U.S. in greater numbers.
The goods and services tax will not contribute to the economy of these municipalities and may very well throw them into an economic turmoil from which they may never recover. Jobs will be lost and, with reforms to the Unemployment Insurance Act, many will not be able to collect benefits and will therefore be forced down to the old welfare office.
Opposition to this goods and services tax is widespread. I believe this government has no option, except to scrap it entirely. Communities in my riding will not survive. In northwestern Ontario, we already pay astronomical prices for gas and transportation services by road and by air.
Fragile industries such as forestry and mining located in single-industry towns will crumble as a result of the goods and services tax on transportation services. Towns such as Ignace, already struggling to survive as a result of mine closures, will become nothing but ghost towns. There will be no jobs, no consumer purchases and therefore, no economic activity.
My constituents are vehemently opposed to the goods and services tax. Petitions are rolling in every day. Now that we know what the government's intentions are with respect to VIA Rail, my constituents realize that the only other mode of transportation left is by air. Many of my constituents are retired citizens. On their pensions, they cannot afford to travel by air. Even if they could, they would not spend that kind of money knowing their pensions are being taxed and that the goods and services tax will mean additional expenses.
The destruction of VIA Rail in northwestern Ontario will mean that many of my constituents will be housebound. Young couples who dream of owning a brand new home, single-parent families trying to make ends meet,
Supply
seniors trying to enjoy their golden years are seeing then-dreams and aspirations destroyed by this government's so-called management of the Canadian economy. They have seen the destruction of universal programs, they have seen the destruction of Canada's passenger rail service and they are seeing the destruction of their future.
Canadians are skeptical of this government, and so they should be. Canadians no longer believe in this government and they know it cannot be trusted any longer. The government may think business is on its side. If the government would only take the time to listen to what business is saying about the goods and services tax, it would soon realize that the support is simply not there. Small business will be faced with an administrative nightmare, and will have to hire additional staff just to sort out the mounds of paper required to administer the GST. Grocery stores will be the hardest hit because they will be trying to figure out where the GST applies and where it does not. Then again, the finance committee chairman has said that the government is reconsidering the tax-free provision for basic groceries.
The goods and services tax has to go. The Canadian economy will not benefit from this tax and Canadians will suffer as a result. Opposition is growing day after day. The government has underestimated the Canadian people. Canadians understand what the goods and services' tax will mean to them and to the economy. Canadians realize that their purchasing power will be significantly reduced. They know that tough times are ahead if the GST goes through. As we always say on this side of the House, Tory times are tough times. Canadians are fed up with carrying the burden of taxation. They want to help reduce the deficit, but they do not want to do it alone. Canadians want to see responsible government.
The constituents of Kenora-Rainy River have spoken out. They have voiced their strong opposition to the reforms to the Unemployment Insurance Act, to the destruction of VIA Rail, to the claw-back provisions of old age security and family allowances and to the goods and services tax. My constituents have told me that the government must scrap the goods and services tax proposal and go back to the drawing board. I think it would be appropriate at this time, considering the fact that there are so many people who consider this a very important issue, that we on this side of the House would

like to propose a motion under Standing Order 26(1). I move:
That, the House continue to sit through the lunch hour for the
purpose of continuing consideration of the business of supply.
I do that, Mr. Speaker, with the hope that the other side will agree to this because I think it is a very important issue and all Canadians would like to hear from their Members of Parliament on this particular issue. I think it would be to our benefit to tighten the belts a little further and stay away from the parliamentary restaurant to speak on behalf of Canadians.
