AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 2 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, the free trade deal has reached the town of Aurora in my federal riding of York North. Sterling Drug Limited recently announced that the drug manufacturing division of the plant will be phased out and 180 workers will lose their jobs as a result of the plant shut-down.
Right after the November 21 election the company closed a sterile product manufacturing division in the plant. Today 40 per cent of the plant will be transferred to the United States of America, 30 per cent to Puerto Rico and only 20 per cent will remain in Canada, simply because this 20 per cent of the products cannot be manufactured anywhere else.
The free trade deal has failed the residents of Aurora. The free trade deal has failed the constituents of the federal riding of York North. The free trade deal has failed Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, Southam News today has reported that Peter Worthington, a journalist and sometime Conservative candidate, acted in 1968 as an informer for the Internal Security Division of the U.S. Department of Justice and for the FBI. This is confirmation not only of Mr. Worthington's lack of simple patriotism to Canada, but of the fact that the U.S. government was spying on Canadians who held different views from that of the U.S. government.
Two days ago Simon Reisman, head of Canada's negotiating team for the free trade deal, said he believed that the U.S. government was spying on the Canadian negotiating team.
Will the government first advise this House whether the government of Canada believes, on the basis of CSIS reports, that the U.S. government is continuing to spy on Canada? Will the government tell the American govern-
September 28, 1989

ment of our outrage at this behaviour? Third, will the Solicitor General make it clear to this House that the government has no intention of emulating this odious practice and sending Canadian spies out into the world to snoop on the friends of Canada?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this week on Parliament Hill there are men and women from across Canada representing many walks of life to remind us that Canada is in need of a new abortion law. They are here to represent the unborn and have a deep love for their country and the province that they represent.
Among this vigilant group is a very special lady by the name of Helen Walsh from Nova Scotia. Mrs. Walsh has recently completed, in August of this year, a walk across this country which started in St. John's, Newfoundland, on Mother's Day, May 8, 1988. This journey totalled 7,700 kilometres.
Mrs. Walsh believes that human life is a gift given by God and that it is unique and special. She holds a concern for the mental, physical and spiritual well-being of both mother and child and believes that faith in our future can only be guaranteed by our witness to a respect for life, from the prebom to the aged.
Mr. Speaker, I commend Mrs. Walsh for her achievement.

Mr. Speaker, the drought program has become a nightmare for producers. Townships and crops which are included change from month to month. Some farmers are even being told to return the interim payments that they received.
This government failed to listen to or understand the arguments put forward by producers and opposition members that the program was flawed, poorly designed and unfair.
I call upon this government to expand the parameters of the appeal process to allow appeals on an individual basis, reconsider its decision to recover any overpayments made in the initial drought payments, and expand
the program to include losses incurred in forage production in 1988.
The government has ruled that farmers producing red clover seed for commercial purposes will be excluded. Producers in my riding are compiling supportive data from independent sources to verify their claims.
I call upon this government to implement the changes I have outlined and give its assurance that red clover producers will be granted an appeal and given a very fair hearing.

1992 ELECTION

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley Valley):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the April 3 Speech from the Throne the government announced plans to organize a major celebration in 1992.
When interviewed, a government official said they had no idea how a number of events in 1992 might be linked.
At a time when pensions are being clawed back, when VIA Rail is being slashed, and when taxpayers are being robbed, this government plans to spend a quarter of a million dollars on a conference in two weeks' time just to help organize the 1992 pre-election party.
The government should advise the House how many staff were involved in the 1992 project, what the theme will be, and how they can justify such an extravagance when ordinary Canadians are being asked to pay more and more every day.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians are told by the Prime Minister that his government is committed to environmentally sustainable development. His actions, unfortunately, contradict such declarations.
A close look at the budget of the environment department reveals that it is very low on the government totem pole. It receives less than 1 per cent of the federal budget and has lost over $50 million to inflation over the past five years. In spite of the fact that the Prime Minister talks of the urgent need for action on global warming, his energy minister continues to support tar sand megaprojects which will increase Canada's carbon dioxide pollution, add to global warming trends, and tie up billions of federal taxpayers' dollars. So far this

government's record on sustainable development consists of high ringing words which are actually hollow because they are not backed by actions.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship); Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, right now Premier David Peterson and his cabinet are considering a proposal which would ruin the last remaining wilderness area in metro Toronto, the Rouge River Valley. Thanks to a group of environmental organizations an Ontario cabinet document was recently made public which calls for the development of the Rouge River Valley.
The people of Scarborough are left asking one simple question. If the four municipalities that border the valley can unanimously support efforts to preserve the Rouge, if the Metro Toronto Conservation Authority can call for saving the Rouge, if the Royal Commission on the Future of Toronto Waterfront can call for saving the Rouge, if close to 50 organizations at the local, provincial and national level can call on saving the Rouge, if the federal government can pledge $10 million toward saving the Rouge, why can David Peterson and his government not take action to save the Rouge?

Mr. Speaker, Newfoundlanders, and I suspect Canadians right across this country, over the last several weeks have been very disappointed to see representatives of the federal government attempting to resolve a matter as critical and pressing as the constitutional evolution of this country by using threats.
We have reports that an official of the federal government in an off the record briefing to the national press suggested that if the province of Newfoundland were to exercise its right as a province to express itself in a matter as important as the Constitution then that province may find itself subject to punishment by the national government.
Nobody has yet apologized to the province of Newfoundland for that kind of threat. The official in question still remains an employee of the federal government and still remains a spokesperson on behalf of the federal government.
To add insult to injury, the Prime Minister himself said yesterday "Wells is ungrateful of Confederation" because of his position on Meech Lake. Newfoundland is not a beggar at the table of Confederation. Newfoundland is a full partner in Confederation and Newfoundland stands solid behind the concept of Canada.
The constitutional question is a difficult one, but let us live together with respect and with dignity, and let us put away the hammers in a resolve to build this nation.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to apprise the House of extremely serious allegations made to me since the Skylink crash in Terrace. I believe there is no option but to pull the operating certificate, initiate a full audit and advise the public that the Dryden inquiry will move as soon as possible to investigate the Terrace crash which killed all seven aboard.
The pilot killed in the crash was time expired. This voids the insurance of the aircraft and the flight. The chief pilot, the brother of the deceased, has now resigned along with the majority of the 402 pilots due to safety concerns. The owner Mr. Raphael Zur, I am advised, has been signing the log books in the place of unqualified pilots. Pilots are flying certain aircraft without proper qualifications. Aircraft are not being properly maintained. Of the three recent gear collapses none of the aircraft have had their engines removed as required.
A 402 recently had to glide into Vancouver International Airport to land due to the failure of the fuel selectors which were installed backward. Pilots have been ordered to fly aircraft after reporting problems to head office. MOT inspectors located a rusted through engine mount on a Metro 2 and yet all three are still in the air without the required engine removal.

A pilot contacted me today and advised me that Mr. Raphael Zur has on several occasions stolen his aircraft for use. The flying public is at risk. On maintenance, on safety, on aviation violations, on Criminal Code matters, falsified logs and lack of insurance the list is long. The Diyden inquiry must take on the Skylink crash.

Mr. Speaker, in Canada today for largely historical reasons there exists a special relationship between aboriginal peoples and the Government of Canada. Within that context it is not surprising that disagreements might arise. Disputes surface in any aspect of human activity. The challenge of leadership is not just to represent your own interests; it is also to know when and how to put disputes to rest.
Earlier this week near Calgary a lengthy dispute between the Sarcee people and the Department of National Defence was resolved. On behalf of all members of the House, who I am sure would wish to join me in this sentiment, I commend the leadership shown by Chief Roy Whitney, the Hon. Bill McKnight, their representatives, and mediator Harold Millican. Their efforts have closed a difficult chapter in relations between CFB Calgary and the Sarcee people. A chapter of renewed trust, hope and commitment has opened.

Mr. Speaker, for the last several months the world has watched as the people of Karabagh and Armenia have struggled to rebuild after the devastation of last December's earthquake. However, over the last several months this rebuilding has been totally frustrated. Azerbaijan has blocked access for all materials and supplies into the earthquake region.
I with others urge the Canadian government to bring this desperate situation to the attention of both the Soviet authorities and to the General Assembly of the United Nations. We ask the Soviets to lift the blockade of Armenia and Karabagh, to ensure the security of the Armenian people in that region, and to hold a referendum in the mountainous Karabagh to determine the majority will in that autonomous region.
Surely the people of Karabagh and Armenia have suffered enough.

Mr. Speaker, the Christmas Tree Producers Association of Lunenburg County will hold their twenty-third annual conference this year at Bridgewater. Collectively, through professionalism, research and hard work, they produce the finest Christmas trees in the world. Every year they export a million and a quarter of these trees bringing millions of dollars to Canadians.
Real Christmas trees are a renewable resource, they are environmentally friendly and they are beautiful. Mr. Speaker, there are only 72 shopping days left before Christmas. This year I urge all Canadians who celebrate Christmas to use real Christmas trees, and none are finer and none are more beautiful than the Christmas trees from Queens and Lunenburg Counties in Nova Scotia.

Mr. Speaker, not long ago, the Vietnamese government announced it would be withdrawing the rest of its troops from Cambodia between September 21 and 26. It also invited foreign observers, including Canadian officials, to watch the operation. Although the withdrawal of the military is heart-warming, we think the Vietnamese authorities can do a lot more to urge Cambodia to agree come to a compromise during this peace process.
Canada's position on observation or peace-keeping missions in Cambodia is well-known. For us to consider taking part in such a mission, all parties involved would have first to arrive at a complete and satisfactory settlement of the problems in Cambodia; our participation must not overly burden Canadian resources and our mandate must be clear and limited in time.
However, Mr. Speaker, since these requirements have not been met, Canada has not seen fit to send an observer.

Oral Questions
We are glad to see that Vietnam has taken steps to withdraw all of its troops from Cambodia and we do hope that this decision will bring us closer to a well-deserved and sustainable peace in Cambodia.

Mr. Speaker, successive governments have stumbled and bumbled their way through office by neglecting a need for a national transportation policy. The challenge is clearly out there for the minister and the government. The Canadian people can accept restraint but they cannot and will not accept a minister and a government which slash services yet offer nothing in the way of a strategy for the future.
Today we do not have a national policy that will propel Canada into the 21st century. Instead we have a disjointed scheme from which we will stumble out of the 20th century. The challenge is clearly up to the minister and this government. If they can meet that challenge and exceed it, they will truly have earned the support of the Canadian people.

Mr. Speaker, the free trade agreement has had a tremendously positive effect on the economy of British Columbia, and my riding of Delta is no exception. Regency Industries is the largest manufacturer of free-standing wood stoves in western Canada and is exporting over 80 per cent of its products, primarily to the U.S. market. Regency has annual sales over $10 million and is predicting a sales increase of 50 per cent over 1988, thanks to the focus on U.S. market potential generated by free trade.
This innovative company is also planning for the future, spending 3 per cent to 4 per cent of revenues on research and development. Exports have already started to Korea and Japan as Regency buys Japanese steel and then ships the finished product back to Japan.
All of Regency's products are approved by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, making these stoves an environmentally friendly product with tremendous growth potential.
This government knew that given the freedom to do so Canadian firms could compete successfully in the world economy. In the export dependent economy of British Columbia no one is proving this adage better than Regency Industries, and I am proud to have that company in my constituency.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. Six and a half million passengers travel more than two billion kilometres a year on VIA Rail, and yet this government is destroying VIA Rail.
I have learned that the government has plans to issue nearly 3,000 pink slips, that is 3,000 lay-off notices, to employees of VIA Rail in the two weeks following Thanksgiving.
At the priorities and planning committee of cabinet on Tuesday the Prime Minister approved a plan to lay off more than 70 per cent of the VIA employees in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, and Newfoundland. VIA operations, particularly in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, will be devastated.
The Prime Minister told the people of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia that they had to use it or lose it. They are using it. Why are they losing it?

Mr. Speaker, I think I should repeat what I said yesterday. The Leader of the Opposition always uses documents that are not official. The Leader of the Opposition has decided on the process of the government. Unfortunately, I must repeat to the Leader of the Opposition that we are in the process of making the decision and in due course we will make the announcement.

Mr. Speaker, did you notice that the Minister did not deny what I suggested to the House? We noticed that very clearly.
I want to just point out one illustration of how irresponsible, calculated, brutal and vicious this government's actions are. Last year in advance of the election the Prime Minister authorized Stewart Mclnnes, who was then the Minister of Public Works, to open a brand new VIA maintenance centre at Halifax at a cost of more than $7 million. Two days ago the Prime Minister

approved a plan to close that brand new maintenance facility in Halifax which cost the taxpayers more than $7 million and employed 150 people. How is that, Mr. Speaker, for pure unadulterated, rank cynicism?
I ask the Prime Minister how much longer he is going to squander the public trust on this particular issue.

Mr. Speaker, of course the Leader of the Opposition can try to mislead Canadians in any way he wishes and say anything he wants.
He can claim that decisions have been made. He can comment on documents that don't exist, without a shred of evidence.
However, I would ask the Leader of the Opposition to be professional about this and to be accurate when referring to official documents about decisions that have been made.
Until those decisions are announced, I would ask him to have the decency to argue on the basis of information that is true, not false.

Mr. Speaker, I agree the decisions have not been announced but they have been made.
I see his colleague, the other "Bouchard", the Minister of the Environment, who didn't have the courage to demand that his colleague order a study-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I know the right hon. gentleman would not want to proceed in an unparliamentary manner, and I would ask him to continue his question keeping that in mind.

Mr. Speaker, why didn't the Minister of the Environment insist that his cabinet colleague from the same part of Quebec order an environmental impact study of the decisions regarding VIA Rail? Because neither the Prime Minister nor the Minister of the Environment have the decency to keep their election promises.
Oral Questions
In any case, will the Prime Minister confirm that last Tbesday he personally approved a lay-off plan for 1,000 VIA Rail employees in Montreal?
Mr. Speaker, I can say that the statement made by the Leader of the Opposition is false.

Mr. Speaker, my question is also directed to the Minister of Transport.
At our public hearings in Quebec on the future of VIA Rail, those who spoke at these hearings all stressed how important it was to have an improved and viable railway service, the operative words being "improved" and "viable".
Will the Minister agree to meet the members of the consultation group set up by the Government of Quebec to examine future prospects instead of laying off thousands of Quebeckers, in Montreal and across the province? Why this negative attitude to VIA Rail?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to welcome the new federal Member from Quebec, and I may say I am pleased the Hon. Member held these hearings. I wonder whether, in the process, he also asked Canadians whether they were prepared pay up to $650 million for a service that is being used by only 3 per cent of Canadians, in Quebec and in the rest of Canada. I think Canadians want sound management of public funds, and that is what we intend to give them, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, in Atlantic Canada alone VIA cuts will kill 500 jobs. A new $7.2 million maintenance facility in Halifax will see its doors closed permanently and thousands of Atlantic Canadians will see the severing of this vital transportation link. Our region has suffered enough under this government's knife.
Will the Prime Minister finally show some compassion and common sense and stop this latest brutal, bloody assault on the people of Atlantic Canada?
Mr. Speaker, I will ask this member, as I did all other members, to wait for the official announcement.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Right Hon. Prime Minister.

Oral Questions
His Minister of Transport in an answer to the Leader of the Opposition said: "He should not base his decision on false affirmations."
The Minister of Transport has been using, much like the rest of the government, erroneous figures to justify the actions that the government is taking. He consistently cites 3 per cent as the number of Canadians who are using rail passenger services. Some 30 per cent to 50 per cent of the users of public carriage, either rail or airplane, is the real figure.
Given that kind of information and given the information that ridership is up, that more people are using VTA Rail, that revenue is up, and that the users are paying for more of the operation, would the Prime Minister not recognize the mistake that his government has made and indicate to this House clearly, and to the people of Canada, that the government will change its mind and will keep VIA rolling?

Mr. Speaker, obviously, those produced by my colleague from the New Democratic Party do not necessarily correspond to the figures that we produced in the Government. I would just point out to him that as far as figures are concerned, Canadian voters twice preferred the Conservatives' figures to the New Democrats'.

Mr. Speaker, my question again is for the Prime Minister. He will know that hundreds of thousands of Canadians have been writing to him and to the Minister of Transport and, in spite of the attempts of the government House leader to circumvent the rule of this House allowing members to send material to the Prime Minister, he has today received hundreds of cards and will receive thousands more during the course of the day from people in support of VTA Rail.
Given that rail passenger service is the safest method of travel and the most environmentally sound method of travel in this country, would he not agree to send the Minister of Transport back to the drawing board to come up with a plan that will allow VTA Rail to continue and to be improved?

Mr. Speaker, I just want to repeat what I said before. The VIA Rail plan which will be proposed will be proposed with regard to the capacity we have to interface this transportation mode with the way people use VIA Rail. People use VIA Rail by 3 per cent, of all intercity travellers use VIA Rail by 3 per cent.
I believe that we will continue to put more than $2 billion over five years in VIA Rail and I believe that is exactly what Canadians can afford at the present time.

Mr. Speaker, poll after poll has indicated that Canadians are willing to support government expenditures that are environmentally sound. I ask the Prime Minister and the Minister of Transport whether they do not realize that this decision about VIA is a major economic decision.
They attend international conferences concerned with hydrocarbons, the greenhouse effect, low level ozone, you name it; and yet here they have a major economic decision which they have not subjected to an environmental assessment. If they did they would find that the environmentally sound thing to do would be to modernize and expand passenger rail service in this country.
Why in the hell can we not have an environmental assessment? Why can the Prime Minister not put his money where his mouth is when it comes to the environment, or shut up about it forever?

Mr. Speaker, I know that this member is worried about the environment, but we can be worried about the environment calmly. I believe that the member should know that the announcement on VIA Rail has not been made yet. When the announcement on VIA Rail is made different parts of the announcement will deal with different concerns. I believe that he should wait for the announcement before giving that kind of performance.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. According to a column written by the Prime Minister's good friend and until very recently senior adviser, Dalton Camp, on September 17, the decision to gut VIA Rail was made in Langevin Block by the estimates review committee chaired by the Prime Minister. I quote: "Benoit Bouchard may still be Minister of Transport but
September 28, 1989

he had no voice in the basic and critical consideration of national transportation policy."
Given that the Minister of Transport cannot possibly have in these circumstances any credibility on this matter, why is the Prime Minister, who chaired the committee that made this decision, refusing to stand in the House and defend these cuts for which the Prime Minister bears primary responsibility?
Mr. Speaker, I have not read the column to which my hon. friend referred-
I'll send you a copy.

The member will send me a copy, I would thank him for that. I have not read the article to which he refers, but I can tell my hon. friend something that is certainly clear to all members of the government and to most Canadians. The present Minister of Transport is widely regarded as a strong and very effective performer here and across the country.
Hear, hear!
In fact, Mr. Speaker, while I haven't read that column, I have read this, and it deals with-
Who wrote it?
Well, I'll tell you. It is in the Sherbrooke Record of July 18, 1988-
July '88-
Oh, oh!

Oh, they want me to keep reading! Let me keep reading then, Mr. Speaker. It is a statement by the Liberal candidate in Sherbrooke, Mr. Wood, who says this in respect to the Conservative candidate, "He brought back the train. Big deal", he says. "Take it away. Nobody is ever on the train. It's always empty," said the Liberal candidate in Sherbrooke.
Hear, hear!
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member has the floor.
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister's endorsement of his Minister of Transport sounds very much like a general's endorsement of the troops before he sends them into the slaughter.
I want to ask the Prime Minister whether or not he agrees with Mr. Camp, his former senior policy adviser, when he says of the decision to gut VIA Rail, "It is a decision that discriminates against the less affluent, the old, the young, the unemployed, the small towns".
Does the Prime Minister agree with his former senior adviser's assessment of this brutal decision? Perhaps this describes the mysterious departure of Mr. Camp from the Langevin Building. Even he has an ounce of salt blood left in his veins and couldn't see his region sold out by this Prime Minister.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to be very clear about-
You weren't even there!
Hear, hear!
Mr. Speaker, I was not there but I am here.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I should remind both the hon. member and the minister that I am here.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I want to be clear. Seriously, the newspaper Le Devoir decision about the cuts to VIA Rail. I believe when a decision is good, is honourable for Canada, and for the Minister of Finance, it is good also for the Minister of Transport.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance told us last night that the goods and services tax would remain steady until 1994, barring unforeseen circumstances.
Mr. Speaker, we have just discussed VIA Rail and certainly that is an example of unforeseen circumstances because last fall, certainly no one expected the disaster that would hit the whole rail system in Canada, especial-

Oral Questions
ly VIA Rail. My question to the Minister, Mr. Speaker, is this:
Can he explain to Canadians exactly what he means when he talks about unforeseen circumstances in the context of his goods and services tax in Canada?

Mr. Speaker, I responded to a question yesterday which asked me about the to the GST. I said that we had put in place, in the last budget, a fiscal track, a fiscal framework that provides for a continuation of program spending at somewhat less than the rate of inflation, a continuation of the revenue picture as it is in place now, including the proposed GST. I said that if we continue in this direction, barring unforeseen circumstances, we will reach the deficit position that is outlined in the budget which involves also a zero cash requirement.

We spoke earlier this week about "wage and price moderation", now it is "unforeseen circumstances". I think Canadians have a right to be more informed on that. I would ask the Minister of Finance this. With high interest rates, high unemployment, high inflation, would recession be an unforeseen circumstance? Would the Minister of Finance try to be very clear on what he means?
First of all, he is talking about 1994 and a tax that has not been imposed yet. Can he clear up the confusion for Canadians as to what he means by unforeseen circumstances?

Mr. Speaker, we have seen over the course of the last few years a number of matters that have happened that had not been anticipated. I think the hon. member would regard as being an unforeseen circumstance the drought in agriculture.
If there is a recession internationally, then that is something that is unforeseen at this time. We have set out what our economic assumptions are in which we base this track. If there is a major deviation from that, then clearly that is an unforeseen circumstance.
As indicated last year at the time of the election, we still do not know what the outlook is for interest rates at any one time. We make assumptions on that, but if there is a major deviation in interest rates either domestically or internationally from the track, then that is something
unforeseen. There are a number of these things that come into play.

My question is also for the Minister of Finance, Mr. Speaker. We know that officials in the minister's department are now looking at various options, various scenarios to reduce the rate of the tax and include food as a taxable item in the GST.
We also know that his buddies on Bay Street are making the same recommendations to the minister and to his officials. This is causing a lot of worry and concern among ordinary Canadians, in particular the senior citizens who built this country, and the poor.
I would like to give the minister one more chance to say in a very categorical way, in an ironclad way, that there will be no tax on basic groceries. Will he say no to his officials, no to his Bay Street buddies, and tell the people of this country that there be no tax on food?
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, let us be quite clear about the reference that the hon. member was referring to. This is not a finance proposal. This is the Department of Finance officials responding to a request for information from members of the research staff of the Finance Committee. They have to respond to these requests, as they would respond to the hon. member if he asked for information. That is the sole basis on which that information is provided.

Mr. Speaker, we have now heard a classic example of the minister evading the question.
What I want from this minister is an ironclad assurance groceries in this country. I ask that in view of the fact that one of his buddies, Laurent Thibeault, came to our committee this morning from the Canadian Manufacturers' Association to complain that there would be a 9 per cent sales tax on power lunches of caviare and champagne-and he wants an exemption. Can the minister assure us that he will not listen to Mr. Thibeault and, instead, assure the ordinary people of this country that there be no tax on basic food?

Mr. Speaker, I made this statement the other day and I will make it again. I am not going to be commenting on individual recom-

mendations that are made by this person or that person before the finance committee. There have been-
-no guarantees.

If the hon. member would listen, Mr. Speaker. There have been recommendations from people who have come before the finance committee to tax food. Others have said keep the exemption in place.
The position of the government, as set out in the proposal that is before the committee now, is that basic groceries are tax-free. We will continue this position. The hon. member can ask me again and again and again, but I will not comment on specific items, specific recommendations that are put before the finance committee until the finance committee has made their recommendations final.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. I want to ask the minister for a clarification on the impact of the GST on our senior citizens.
There was a lot of information in the riding of Elk Island and, indeed, across this country regarding the impact of the GST on our seniors. Some of this information good, some of it is misleading, but all of it is very confusing. Let us clarify this issue once and for all.
Mr. Minister, what will be the impact of the GST on our senior citizens?
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I think as colleagues understand the change from the existing federal sales tax to the goods and services tax is a major step forward in the impact of sales taxes on our senior citizens. Sales taxes have been widely regarded as regressive, but with the change from the federal sales tax to the goods and services tax we will have for the first time a progressive sales tax system because of the implementation of a very substantially increased goods and services tax credit.
In addition to that, we have exempted a number of other things in the GST tax proposals, such as medical devices. That includes hearings aids as well as glasses, health care, prescription benefits-

What about protheses?
Oral Questions

-protheses, homemakers' services that are provided by non-profit institutions, meals-on-wheels, and a wide range of things like that. That is why the goods and services tax system as a whole is very good for our senior citizens.

Mr. Speaker, recently our government announced the release of the drug AZT for the treatment of AIDS. I understand that there has been a recent development. I was wondering if our Minister of Health could tell us what the most recent developments are in the treatment of AIDS in Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Perrin Beatty (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to inform the House today that DDI will be available under the Emergency Drug Release Program. It will be available to Canadians who are symptomatic of AIDS and HIV infection and who are intolerant of AZT. It will be available free of charge under a program administered by the manufacturer.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Justice. During the public hearings on the unemployment insurance bill which end today, serious doubt has been raised with respect to the constitutionality of this bill, in view of the fact that the bill provides that up to 15 per cent of unemployment insurance moneys can be used for training and development purposes.
The minister knows that federal jurisdiction in unemployment insurance is the result of a constitutional amendment in 1940, which very specifically refers to unemployment insurance and not to training and development.
In order to clear the air on this point, would the minister order an independent legal opinion, make a commitment to this House to make that opinion public, and ask the government to delay this bill until this constitutional issue has been resolved?

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill was, naturally,

September 28, 1989
Oral Questions
reviewed by justice officials prior to introduction. We take the position that the act is constitutional and is within federal powers.

Mr. Speaker, that is unfortunate. I guess we will have to pursue that issue ourselves.
I have a supplementary question for the Prime Minister. It concerns the area of federal-provincial relations.
Another major issue being raised in the committee by many, many witnesses is the shift of the unemployed from the unemployment insurance system to provincial welfare rolls. As a result of this bill, thousands of unemployed Canadians will be left without unemployment insurance and the responsibility will be shifted to the social assistance systems.
In Toronto, the estimated increase in the welfare budget is $10 million. In the regional municipality of Ottawa, the estimated increase in the welfare budget is $10 million. In Sudbury it is $2 million.
I want to ask the Prime Minister if he would meet with the provincial premiers in order to get an exact estimate on how this bill will increase provincial welfare budgets. Would he delay the bill until he has those estimates, discussed them and put them before the House?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister of State (Employment and Immigration) and Minister of State (Seniors)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Seniors); Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to repeat that the unemployment insurance system will not be cut back; what we want to do as a government is to improve it, make it more efficient and more equitable.
As far as social assistance is concerned, we already have a joint program with Quebec and as part of unemployment insurance reform, we already provided additional funds to be shared between the provincial and federal governments. Measures have already been taken to create more jobs by training the workers needed for new requirements.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. By the end of
this month, tomorrow or Monday, the Hache Thsk Force on the Scotia-Fundy is expected to submit its report to the cabinet committee which he set up to examine the current crisis in the Atlantic ground fishery. Virtually every witness who has appeared before this committee, including the Nova Scotia Department of Fisheries, has complained that the groundfish management system, "-has focused on establishing, allocating and enforcing quotas but not on the managing of the fishery".
Will the Prime Minister ensure and order immediate direction to the cabinet committee to look at the Hache report to formulate proposals that will relieve the hardship currently being experienced by the thousands of people who are connected to the inshore fishery and the Scotia-Fundy region?

Hear, hear!
Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and
Oceans): Mr. Speaker, I can assure the hon. member that I am seriously considering the findings of the study of the special task force conducted by Jean Hache. In fact, I received a full briefing on his report only yesterday.
We have had a number of very positive recommendations from the fishermen in the area on improving science and the quality of data we receive from fishermen as an input to our management process, and the changes of gear which were necessary; but, above all, the importance of dealing with a huge over-capacity problem in southwest Nova Scotia. I will be taking recommendations to cabinet to deal with that in due course.

Mr. Speaker, the cabinet committee was set up by the Prime Minister to study the total. It was taken out of the hands of the Minister of Fisheries. I am asking that immediate attention be given to the Hache report.
My supplementary is to the Minister. I want to ask him whether the hardships that his policies have inflicted over the past two summers of no work for the people- the thousands of people in the inshore fishery-and whether the evidence of the Hache report has finally convinced him that his management plan, as the Department of Fisheries of the Province of Nova Scotia has said, has focused on the wrong areas and not focused on the managing of the fisheries on the east coast. It shows up in the northern cod, on which the cabinet committee
September 28, 1989

is meeting, and also on other policies of this particular committee.

In fact, Mr. Speaker, the Hache findings suggest possible new regulations and changes in fishing methods which would involve tighter control by the Department of Fisheries and Oceans. Secondly, on my first review of the report, it appears that in the present year there are no extraordinary circumstances of hardship which are unlike those of previous years with the exception of lower prices and the problems created by exchange rates. There are no areas of unemployment which cannot be accommodated, Mr. Speaker, within the existing programs that are provided by the federal government.

Mr. Speaker, since last April the government has been telling Canadians that not many people would be hurt by the unemployment insurance cuts. They said only 30,000 people would be unable to obtain benefits. Statistics Canada has contradicted the government. It says that 130,000 people will lose all of their benefits. Thirty times more people will be hit in Newfoundland alone than the government has admitted to.
My question is for the Prime Minister. Would the Prime Minister confirm that by Statistics Canada's own analysis there will be 130,000 Canadians who will lose all their benefits? Would he also confirm that his government's own stats have been a dramatic understatement?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister of State (Employment and Immigration) and Minister of State (Seniors)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Seniors); Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to tell my colleague that since our Government took office, we have created 1,500,000 jobs, including 878,000 for women. I repeat that what we are trying to do with unemployment insurance reform is to make this system fair and equitable by taking account of regional disparities.
I come from a region that is affected by unemployment and we have implemented a measure that will respect the worker who wants to work.
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, I think I will have to try and address my supplementary question to the minister. She is not answering the question. She knows that Statistics Canada did not make up those figures. She knows those numbers are right, but that her department has not had the guts to release how the numbers are being cooked up.
Is the minister telling us that she was really not aware of the horrible impact these measures would have? Was she aware of them and did the government still allow incorrect numbers to be released?

Mrs. Vezina Mr. Speaker, I personally was responsible for the Department that oversees Statistics Canada and I have confidence in Statistics Canada's data.
I also know that the data I just quoted you truly reflect the job creation situation. The unemployment insurance program will continue to be a safety net for the working man or woman seeking employment. And what we are trying to do as a responsible government is to ensure that most Canadians will be able to find work in the new markets of the year 2000. We are preparing the future.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. It is a given that cuts are going to be made to VIA Rail. Keeping that in mind, Mr. Speaker, what indication can the minister give this House that both he and the government will be bringing forward a national transportation policy that will lead Canada into the 21st century?
Also, Mr. Speaker, aside from debt reduction, I want to know what innovative measures does the minister envisage to propel us into the 21st century? Will we have a national transportation policy to address the real needs of this nation?

Mr. Speaker, I thank my friend for the question. I think there are two very important points here. The first is that, of course, the reason why we have to intervene with VIA

Oral Questions
Rail is because we cannot any longer waste Canadian money as we did for such a long time.
Second, I believe one thing we have to determine in the transportation policy is to have better management of the rail system. When we move in that direction and it is done, Mr. Speaker, I believe then will be the time also to determine a broader perspective in terms of transportation in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, we now know of a major source of foreign investment in Canada, illegal drug money from the United States. A confidential report released in Washington yesterday confirms what we predicted two years ago. Canada has become a major haven for laundering hundreds of millions of dollars a year in dirty drug money.
My question is to the Prime Minister. If his government is truly serious about fighting the drug war, will his government immediately introduce legislation to require Canadian banks and institutions to report large cash and foreign currency transactions as a means of stopping the laundering of illegal drug money in Canada?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to commend the Hon. Member for raising an issue which has to be of great concern to all the members of this House. As he knows, it is of great concern to this government, and we have already acted.
I would like to remind the hon. gentleman that effective January 1,1989, we brought amendments to the Canada Criminal Code and the Food and Drugs Act which made money laundering in Canada a criminal offence.
At the Toronto economic summit in 1988 Canada played a prominent role in achieving agreement on a set of principles and initiatives which will result in greater co-operation. Even last week my colleague, the Minister of Finance, raised the issue at the summit.
With our American neighbours we have made arrangements for mutual legal assistance. The Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions has instructed all banks to institute procedures to detect money laundering. I could go on for a long time. I think we have taken very decisive action.
Hear, hear!
I assure the Hon. Member the report was based on data which is not relevant any more.

Mr. Speaker, my question is also to the Solicitor General. TTie last response did not show any mechanisms developed and being used by banks.
In view of the government's failure to date to impose mechanisms to track profits of the international drug cartel through our Canadian financial institutions, I want to know when the government is going to show some leadership, stop dragging its feet and offer to us a comprehensive and effective Canadian initiative in the war against drugs. Or do we have to wait for the FBI or the Drug Enforcement Administration to show us how?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to reassure the Hon. Member that we do not need to wait for anybody. At this very moment the banks, with the office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions and the RCMP, are working on very precise measures to modernize our methods. We are very confident that we can tackle that.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Supply and Services. On May 24, Westinghouse Canada announced the closure of its Renfrew, Ontario plant. At that time we were told that with the exception of some specific equipment, the rest of the equipment would remain in the plant until the end of the year to allow it to be sold as a going concern.
However, those Westinghouse officials have gone back on their word during the summer. As a result we have lost one potential buyer because equipment was not available with the plant. We do not want to lose another one.
Is there any recourse the Minister has with regard to the procurement of goods and services from Westinghouse, given the current Westinghouse withdrawal from Renfrew and, more particularly, the manner in which they are doing so?
September 28, 1989

I would hope that they would certainly negotiate in good faith with upcoming potential purchasers of this facility, and that they would leave their equipment in place as they promised they would do.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology. Given the several millions of dollars in federal grants, training programs and tax credits that the Minister of Supply and Services mentioned that have gone into the plant over the past nine years, and because much of this was done in the name of regional development, in a sincere way, does the minister not agree, both morally and realistically, that this government-subsidized equipment should be available to a prospective buyer who will remain in the Renfrew area so that the benefits that were meant for this slow growth region will in fact remain in that area and be of benefit to hundreds of people as intended in the first place?

The member for Mackenzie, and this will be the last question and supplemental.
Oral Questions DROUGHT PROGRAM

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Agriculture. Prior to the drought cheques being mailed out this summer, the minister and his officials repeatedly assured producers of commercial forage seeds, the grasses, clovers and alfalfas, that they would be receiving drought payments. When the cheques came the commercial producers were dropped from the program and only producers of pedigreed seed were left in.
Will the minister explain why commercial producers were not paid on either the same basis as the pedigreed producers, on the basis of the quota book acreage, or even using a basket-of-commodity approach which was built into the program? Why were the producers of commercial grasses, clovers and alfalfas left out of the drought program even though they were badly affected?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):

Mr. Speaker, my understanding is that this would have been very difficult to administer. Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is for the Minister of the Environment who monitors all government programs to make certain that they are environmentally friendly.
Can the minister explain why he accepted this decision by the Department of Agriculture which harms the country's long term ability to protect the environment by signalling to producers of commercial forage seeds, the alfalfas, clovers, and grasses, that these seeds and plants are not useful to stop soil erosion and to clean up the air and the water of our country? Why did he stand by and do nothing?

process that we are going through. I would invite the hon. member's support in that particular initiative and we will welcome any comments or suggestions that he has to make in that regard.

subsubtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR STANDING COMMITTEE TO TRAVEL
speechtext:
With the consent of the House, Mr. Speaker, I would like to revert to motions. With the consent of all parties in the House, I would like to put to you the following motion on the business of the Standing Committee on Finance:
That the House hereby directs the following arrangements with respect to the consideration, by the Standing Committee on Finance, of the proposed goods and services tax
1.	That the committee be authorized to travel as follows:
A)	A sub-committee of the said committee, composed of one member from each recognized party in the House, to travel to Whitehorse, for hearings on Sept. 30, 1989;
B)	The full committee to travel for hearings in Vancouver, (October 2 and 3), in Edmonton (Oct. 4), in Regina (Oct. 5), in Winnipeg (Oct. 6), in St. John's, (Oct. 18), in Halifax (also on Oct. 18), in Charlottetown (Oct. 19), and Fredericton (also on Oct. 19).
2.	That the committee make its report to the House no later than Thursday, November 28, 1989.
3.	That televised broadcasting of any or all public meetings of the committee in Ottawa, subsequent to the adoption of this order and until the committee enters into its report, be on the basis of the principles and practices now governing broadcast of the proceedings of the House of Commons.
4.	That the order for consideration by the House of second reading and committee referral of any bill or bills relating to the proposed goods and services tax be for "second reading and referral to the Standing Committee on Finance."
5.	That the committee be authorized to travel to Mont Ste. Marie, Quebec from November 6 to November 9 inclusive for the purpose of drafting the said report.

I gave notice to the Speaker during Question Period of my desire to raise a point of privilege regarding a matter that occurred during Question Period.
Myself and members of my caucus erroneously used the services of Pages to deliver material to the Prime Minister's desk. It is my understanding that the normal procedure, and I am not sure if it is an order of the House, is that large mailings of that nature should go to the post office.
In this modem era we all know that mail such as that really does not come to the attention of the person it is addressed to. It ends up in a computer somewhere and perhaps a list of the number of letters received each week is provided to the intended recipient.
I would like to ask, Mr. Speaker, if you could undertake to review that particular rule so that members of Parliament, on behalf of their constituents, can have direct access in terms of large quantities. Obviously, we still have the right to send an individual letter over to a Minister or to the Prime Minister, and vice versa. At one o'clock when the House rose there were five minutes left for questions and comments on the speech of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River.
The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James on questions and comments.
Mr. Harvard I was listening to my colleague from Kenora-Rainy River and it raised a question in my mind with respect to the inflationary pressure that would be brought on by imposition of the GST. I think the finance minister has already indicated in a number of statements that inflation would rise as a result of the levying of the GST. That in turn would probably raise interest rates and reduce our purchasing power.
The question I have for my colleague from Kenora- Rainy River has to do with what impact this is going to have on wage rates in the country. What is the response going to be from unions? What is the response going to be from ordinary workers? If they face inflation, if they face higher interest rates, if they face a loss of purchasing power, are' they not going to go to their employers asking for huge raises to offset this GST?
That is the question I have for my friend from Kenora-Rainy River.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my hon. friend for his question. I shall preface my answer with a little background, and being a unionist myself, it gives me great pleasure to tell you that I have had discussions with some unions relating to their philosophy of how they are going to bargain once there is GST, if it so unluckily does pass.
Basically, they are not going to accept it and just allow their way of living, their improvements in life, and what they expect for their family to go unquestioned. What they will do, I am sure, when bargaining in the next round of negotiations, and some are coming up this year with very large, major unions, is expect a large increase in wages to offset the loss of their income.
I expect what you will see is a confrontation between business and labour. As you all know, it is important for labour, and the individuals who work for the different labour movements, to get the same improvements in wages as the businessman would. Therefore, he will pass
September 28, 1989

it on to the consumer. I think what we will see is mass inflation in our country because there will be an out and out war between labour and business.

I have a question for my colleague from Kenora-Rainy River. First, I would like to congratulate him on an excellent presentation. I did note in his presentation that he highlighted two areas that certainly are of interest to me, small business and tourism. I would like to ask my hon. friend if he could highlight some of his more pointed concerns, particularly in these areas of small business and in tourism.

Mr. Speaker, in an area like northwestern Ontario there are many small communities which are basically single-industry towns, except for the area of tourism, which is the secondary industry that we have. We have been told over and over by different governments, and this government is no exception, that tourism and the service industry is the industry of the future, that is where we should be headed, where we should be looking to in the next century.
Unfortunately, that is not taking place in places like northwestern Ontario in the tourism industry. I might say before going on that the Minister responsible for Small Businesses and Tourism did come to northwestern Ontario this summer and told all the tourist operators that he had the ear of the Minister of Finance and that there would be no problems in relation to the tourism industry. They would be looked after. There would be exceptions and exemptions for them. Lo and behold in the technical paper there is no such thing. Tourism is a big employer in regions like northwestern Ontario because of its beauty and the fact that people like to visit.
What has happened now is that the goods and service tax will increase the cost of transportation, it will increase the cost of goods, and it will increase the cost of staying in hotels and motels. That effect will run off what little tourism is left in northwestern Ontario.
What we are finding now, and these figures will bear this out, is that there is a 50 per cent drop in the number of people crossing the border from the United States to Canada. In our area tourists are dropping back because they are now going to places like northern Minnesota, which is very similar to northwestern Ontario, because it is cheaper and it is easier to have an affordable holiday, whereas in Canada we have made it too restrictive
Supply
because of the tax increases that keep coming every time we turn around.
It is easy for the people in Toronto or Montreal to say: "Well, it is okay. One cent more for gasoline."
When you use vehicles as much as we do to go hundreds of miles from one neighbour to the next, it is very expensive. When tourists are put in that situation and they figure out how much it is going to cost to go on their holiday, with the travelling involved, they suggest to their families that because of their pocketbooks it is just not affordable. Therefore they go somewhere else like northern Minnesota which is not doing us any good. To add insult to injury we are now going to lose VIA Rail, a big tourist promoter in northwestern Ontario, which also brings megabucks as does tourism in our area. So now we have the double whammy.
Therefore, I suggest that we cannot afford this goods and services tax, not in northwestern Ontario, not anywhere in Canada. I suggest that the Minister of Finance take a different approach and look at stimulating the economy through different mechanisms rather than raising taxes over and over again.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate today because I think it is important that we put some of these statements that have been made about the goods and services tax into some perspective.
There have been some who have said that this tax is something that has been dreamed up at the last minute and put before the Canadian people. Nothing could be further from the truth, because back in November of 1984, in the agenda paper for economic renewal, I did state for the first time on behalf of the government that this was a tax that we were considering. It was all part of the economic plan that we put forward at that time. It was a plan designed to reduce the deficit, to get out debt under control, to improve the operations of the economy by giving encouragement to the private sector through deregulation, through encouragement of investment, through change in our privatization policy, freeing up markets, getting access to the large United States market, as well as the multilateral trade negotiations. It was also designed to help Canadians get better training and

September 28, 1989
Supply
get better equipped to face the future. All of this is combined with tax reform as well.
We have had the first stage of tax reform that became effective in 1988 for personal income tax and corporate income tax. Now we are moving in a systematic way to the second stage of tax reform, sales tax reform. We all know in this House that this goods and services tax that we are proposing is a replacement for an existing tax which is a very damaging tax to our economy. There are very good reasons why we are moving in this direction. The existing tax results in a hidden tax on our exports. The nature of the tax results in a one-third less burden of taxation on imports as opposed to Canadian production. Canada is the only country in the world today that still has a manufacturers' sales tax. Forty-eight countries have a multi-stage tax such as the one that we are proposing here, so we are not exactly pioneers in this area. It is something that has been a long time coming and it is important that we get on to this so we can remove this drag from our economy which is causing us to lose about $9 billion of economic activity every year.
There are very good reasons to bring in this new tax. One is the competitive position as I have just described. The second is to allow us to get on further in getting the deficit down and controlling our debt. Finally, since we all pay taxes, and we all know we have to pay taxes, the important consideration and the key responsibility of government is to bring in a fair effective tax. That is what we are doing with the goods and services tax.
Now opposition members have said in their interventions earlier today that everybody is opposed to this tax, and that the tax is fundamentally flawed. One thing absolutely clear is that no fundamental structural flaw has been pointed out in this tax proposal. In the month and a half in which the technical paper has been out for the practitioners to study, no fundamental structural flaws have been pointed out.
Opposition members have said: "Let us scrap it. Let us get back to the drawing boards". As I said a minute ago, governments have been trying since the early 1950s to get rid of this existing tax. Mr. MacEachen, the Minister of Finance in 1981, made a proposal to get rid of the tax
and move it to the wholesale level. That did not work, but he did ask for Mr. Wilf Goodman, Q.C., to head a committee that would advise on the way we should be moving from the manufacturers' sales tax to a new type of consumption tax. In essence what Mr. Goodman proposed, moving to a multi-stage tax at the retail level, is the precise form of taxation that we are talking about today.
After Mr. Goodman reported to the government, we brought out a white paper in June, 1987 and we are proceeding with consultations and discussions with many groups and organizations to fine tune and make sure that the proposal we have on the table today represents the consensus that we could achieve as we designed this tax.
What I would like to do is analyse what people are saying. In the finance committee people have said that hardly anyone agrees, but it is very clear that there is a common theme running through here, namely, that practically everyone has said get rid of the old tax. People have some problems with the proposal that is on the table today, and when one analyses exactly what they are saying, it is very clear that some have come down on one side or the other side of the particular issue. Yes, both sides are opposed, but they also have diametrically opposing points of view. People have said they want to recommend change by lowering the rate, by changing the credit, by changing the tax base, and by reducing the compliance costs. Yes, there is this criticism, but let us examine it further.
How would those who want to reduce the rate go about doing that? By reducing the credit? By reducing the small business payment, or offsetting the compliance costs? Would they do it by reducing the housing rebate? Some people have been saying we should reduce those things.
But on the other side we have the small business community saying: "You have got to pay more on the compliance offset". The housing industry is saying "You have to raise the housing rebate". Others have said we have to increase the size of the tax credit.
We have very clearly conflicting points of view. We have people who are saying it is important that we reduce the complexity of the tax. One of the elements of complexity is whether or not groceries should be taxed.
September 28, 1989

We have some people who are saying "Yes, tax everything. Groceries should be taxed". On the other hand, we have the grocery association and some of the organizations representing the lower-income people, people on welfare, who are saying "By no means should you tax food".
Again we have people saying tax food and others saying don't tax food. We have people saying exempt me, exempt the product that I sell while we have people who are saying tax everything. That is the position we have seen develop over the course of the last few weeks. There is criticism, but that criticism is also diametrically opposed.
I want to comment on one thing that the Leader of the Opposition said today. I could not believe my ears. He said "This government has lost complete control of spending". How can this man talk about completely losing control of spending when, as finance minister, his government's spending increased at a rate of 29 per cent in one of the years in which he was minister of finance. The program spending of the Government of Canada prior to our taking office was increasing at 5 per cent higher than the rate of inflation, 14 per cent per annum. Compare that to this government which he says has totally lost control of spending. Our program spending has increased at 3.5 per cent per annum, a half per cent below inflation, rather than the 5 per cent above inflation under the previous government.
People-including I believe the Leader of the Opposition-have said that this is the most regressive form of taxation.
When we came into office we had a sales tax system that resulted in low-income Canadians paying two or three percentage points more of their income in tax than people in upper incomes. Now, with the GST tax system including the tax, the low-income credit and the middle-income tax reduction, we have the exact opposite. People with low income are paying two or three percentage points less of their income in sales tax than people with upper incomes. Rather than moving into a more regressive tax system, we have moved into a progressive tax system in sales tax reform.
Supply
The NDP said that it would never impose a consumption tax. I do not know where the member from Kamloops was when the NDP signed the finance committee report which said, "In short, a single rate value added tax on the broadest possible base is a desirable objective." Does the broadest possible base include things like children's clothing and services? I would like him to describe what they had in mind when they signed that report as to what the broadest possible base is, because we have an example here of politicians talking out of both sides of their mouths. I think Canadians are getting a little fed up with that type of reaction from their political members.
Let me get back to the essential point of my intervention today. The government position as set out in the technical paper that we put forward on August 8 is a proposal which has been developed after much study and careful consultation since June, 1987, when we put out the white paper on tax reform. We consulted with the provinces for about two years. The result was the technical paper, a very specific proposal which took into account the balancing interests about which we had discussions during this period of time.
We expect opposition and we expect different points of view. It is the responsibility now of the government and of the committee to reconcile these points of view. It is the responsibility of the opposition not to blindly repeat each piece of criticism but to join in this debate, to join in this discussion. I call upon the opposition members and the public to engage in this debate so that together we can develop the best form of sales tax system in the world today.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to what the minister had to say, having sat through the hearings of the finance committee for the last number of days. Many of his comments on what the witnesses were saying are certainly of interest to me.
I would like to point out to him that even the staunchest supporters of the tax, the ones who have said you should go ahead with it, have been adamant in pointing out the flaws. Even those who think you should tax everything that moves-we were told this morning you should tax the interest on the bank accounts-say

September 28, 1989
Adjournment Debate
that we cannot live with a two-tiered tax if the government cannot get the provinces on side. This is, in the words of the retail council last night, an act of self-mutilation.
We heard on the news last week that this government in fact had-and I suppose still does-a proposal in its back pocket that would allow an amendment of the manufacturers' sales tax to continue a tax only at the federal level so we would not get into this incredible mess that we are leading into with a two-tiered system of consumption tax in Canada.
Whatever other flaws there are in this proposal, and there are many, the fact that we cannot have a single-tiered tax system in this country makes it impossible to go ahead with this proposal.
I think the minister should admit that. He should get up and say: "This is the best we can do but it is not good enough and, therefore, we will have to find another way to address the inequalities and the problems in the manufactures' sales tax". The best minds in Canada will have to address themselves on how to fix that tax because we have to live with this federal system.
In fact, as we heard this morning in the committee, it is really the monetary policy which this government is pursuing that is hurting our exporters a lot more than the manufacturers' sales tax. It adds 1.2 per cent to the price of an export. In the last 23 months the exchange rate of the Canadian dollar has gone from 67 cents U.S. to 85 cents U.S.
That is a much greater problem to the exporters than the manufacturers' sales tax. Yet the government does nothing to address the problem of high interest rates in Canada. I would like the minister to tell us whether it is true, as the reports have suggested, that the Department of Finance had prepared for him a proposal to amend the manufacturers' sales tax at the federal level only without going to a multi-stage value added tax.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is absolutely right. That was roundly criticized by all members of the finance committee in the last Parliament. Surely, the government would be criticized roundly if we did not listen to the views of the finance committee. That is why we have not proceeded with that
and why we are proceeding with the goods and services tax.
The hon. member asks why are we not dealing with the problem of high interest rates. We are, Mr. Speaker. But we are not doing it in the way that was dealt with by the government 10 years ago.
I remind the hon. member that we had an inflation problem in the 1970s. The rate of inflation in 1976 was about the same as it is now, 5.5 per cent. About four years later it was up at 13 per cent because the government of the day swept it under the carpet. We are addressing this head on with our monetary policy. It involves for a while high interest rates, higher than I would like to see, higher than the hon. member would like to see. But I know it is necessary for us to endure these rates for a period of time so we can get that problem of inflation under control.
If we do not get inflation under control, we will be standing here in the House talking about 13 per cent unemployment and the 20 per cent interest rates that we had in the early 1980s. This government is not going to repeat those mistakes. We are going to deal with the problem of inflation now and not sweep it under the carpet. We learn from past mistakes that others have made. We do not blindly follow the shibboleths that my hon. friend would like us to.

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
speechtext:
It is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 38, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: the Hon. Member for Winnipeg Transcona- The Environment- VIA Rail cutbacks-Request for impact study / Government position; the Hon. Member for Algoma-Dairy industry; the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan-Transportation-VIA Rail services / Government position.
September 28, 1989

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Thmer (Vancouver-Quadra) that:
That this House condemns the Government for its mismanagement
of the Canadian economy, including:
1) the threat to impose a new 9 per cent sales tax that is regressive, inequitable, invisible and inflationary; 2) an unjustifiable high interest rate policy, with an interest rate spread between Canada and the United States that is at record highs; 3) negligence in the management of Canadian trade causing unparalleled reductions in our trade balance and a loss of jobs, and threatening the survival of many formerly thriving Canadian industries; 4)abandonment of Canadian primary producers with resulting undermining of the farming, fishing and forest industries; and 5) continued neglect of regional disparities.

I am very pleased to be able to stand up today and speak on the economy. But like the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition I am saddened and disappointed that I have to speak on such a sombre note.
There is so much to talk about, it is difficult to know where to begin. I could talk about the disastrous effect of the GST like many others have done today. I could talk about the disillusionment of the 2.5 million senior citizens at the clawback. I could talk about the dramatic decline of the federal direct assistance to business in Atlantic Canada, the anxiety of fishermen over the future of the fisheries on both coasts, the increasingly destructive effect of the high interest rates to which reference was just made. There is also the fact that during the second quarter of the year over-all economic growth hit the skids along with exports, corporate profits, housing starts, auto and retail sales. Even the tourism deficit hit a historic high of $1 billion. That is a large percentage of the whole business.
Yesterday we sat in this house and heard in disbelief that the government leaked plans to slash VIA Rail. I could express my concern and that of my colleagues over the 31 times our taxes have been increased by the Minister of Finance since 1984, in most cases without telling us what was going on.
Supply
I could talk about this government's policy of removing almost all barriers to foreign investment in which foreign buyers have enthusiastically responded, or the reports that there have been 23 Canadian companies sold to U.S. buyers during the first six months of this year compared with 11 during the first half of 1988.
I could talk about Canada's 514,000 full-time university students who are resuming their studies at 68 degreegranting institutions this fall, for whom overcrowded classrooms, outdated equipment and deteriorating building plants are a fact of life. I could talk about the million youngsters in this country that will never be able to be the teachers, professors, engineers and leaders that they have the potential to be because of the economic circumstances.
I could highlight the concern that free trade is costing us control of our economy. I could use as examples, unfortunate examples, the unexpected and the ironic twist in which the government is being forced to buckle under a free trade bilateral deliberation that threatens Canadian restrictions on the export of fish in British Columbia and threatens that industry, 4,000 jobs and $580 million worth of exports.
I am more concerned as the member for Bonavista- Trinity-Conception, that this will go on to threaten the east coast fishing industry. It is hard to know where to start and where to end. We are all the victims of time and circumstances in this House, so I would like to concentrate on two aspects of the economy that concern me the most: The changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act, Bill C-21, and the goods and services tax.
First, Bill C-21. There are a number of things that concern me about this deplorable initiative of the government to divert $1.3 billion from the $13 billion fund in the near term and to eventually withdraw all government support of the future to the tune of what is now $2.9 billion.
There are individual concerns, but, above all, it is the negative synergism of all these concerns taken together. In this case, the individual points add up to more than the sum of the parts. They add up to something like 10 or 12 times the effect, and the effect is not linear, it is more like exponential.

Supply
Let me outline the results of the proposed changes that concern me and practically every person involved with unemployment insurance in the riding of Bonawis-ta-Trinity-Conception, the province of Newfoundland, Atlantic Canada and perhaps all over the country. First of all it represents a breach of trust. It is a broken promise solemnly made by this government last fall. It redirects money for the unemployed into training. There is nothing wrong with training but why should it come out of the unemployment insurance fund? More important, it is training for jobs and positions that do not exist in my riding. I do not see them ever existing.
It provides the level playing field by getting the government out of the UIC business, insisted on by the free trade agreement for the benefit of the United States, not for the benefit of Canada.
It hurts the very people it was designed to protect. It was sudden; it was abrupt; and it attacks the very heart of the Canadian social security system, a program about which Canadians care very deeply. It runs counter to the expectations of Canadians. As if that were not bad enough, this is at a time when the Minister of Finance himself admits that next year the unemployment rate will run from 7.7 per cent to 8.5 per cent, a 10 per cent increase in one year. He promises that next year we we are going to have a 3 per cent rise in inflation. We add all this up with the unemployment insurance changes, and it is not a very bright picture.
Taken all together, they spell disaster. This is the constitutional right about which Canadians concern themselves, and the government has attempted to privatize it. That is just not honest. The questions has been raised here today about whether or not this is lawful. There is no doubt that it is unjust. Perhaps unlawful justice is done and lawful injustices are committed somewhere in the world every day, but this is Canada. We do not have to stand for that and we will not.
