And we won't.

No, we won't. During the election campaign the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition was accused by this government of using tactics to scare Canadians. They said he was wrong. He warned that the free trade agreement risked major changes to our social
programs because our senior negotiators admitted that they did not have the time to work out the definition of regional development and subsidies.
Well, he was right and they were wrong. He was right because what he said might happen is happening. They were wrong for two reasons. First of all, they broke their promise. More importantly to me and many of my constituents, they knew they would break that promise even as they were saying the opposite at the time. That is nothing short of despicable. They cannot be trusted.
I want to take a few minutes to talk about my concerns over the goods and services tax. More and more, I find my reaction to this terrible proposal-there is only one term that I can use- inexpressively distressing. It is nothing more than a cash cow that will raise wages, fuel inflation, cripple small business and drive consumers crazy right out of their minds.
I spoke about my concerns earlier in this House on June 15. Three months later, my concerns are greater. The more I learn about what the government thinks it has in mind, the more concerned I become. Is it any wonder I am concerned? The government said this was going to be revenue neutral. The very first statement in its shameful attempt to bribe Canadians with their own money into accepting this bill of goods is the following statement: "It is going to be revenue neutral and it is a major part of the ongoing program to reduce the deficit".
I am confused. The government said it was going to be done in co-operation with the provinces. Not one province agrees. The government said it is going to be visible. We see it is not visible. It is going to be simple. Somebody estimated, I think it was the Consumers' Association of Canada, that 10,000 bureaucrats will be needed to administer it and somewhere in the vicinity of billions of dollars.
Let me look at the experience of some other countries very quickly. Denmark, same tax, 10 per cent to 22 per cent; France, 13.6 per cent to 18.6; Germany, 10 per cent to 14 per cent; New Zealand, 10 per cent to 12.5 per cent; Britain, 10 per cent to 15 per cent; Holland, 12 per cent to 20 per cent and, Sweden, 10 per cent to 24.5 per cent. If we follow the example of Sweden, we would be able to cancel all income taxes and get the same revenue. That

is a startling revelation and perhaps I should not reveal it to this government.
Everybody is against this tax. Eighty per cent of Canadians are against it according to a recent poll. As far as I am concerned and from what I hear today, the world is against it. We have a saying in Newfoundland that I would like to trot out for the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance. It is a very simple statement. They say: "In a fight between yourself and the world, back the world".
Mr. Reid Mr. Speaker, it is a great privilege to be back here and to have the opportunity to respond to my hon. friend and fellow Newfoundlander who, I should like to point out to this House, was very kind to me recently during some time that I spent in his beautiful and historic constituency. Unfortunately, that does not make up for what we have heard in the last ten minutes from my friend opposite who wanted to talk about this government's policy in terms of the economy.
This government's policy let us see in this country the creation of 1,550,000 jobs since September, 1984. The national unemployment rate is falling from 11.6 per cent to 7.4 per cent and the youth unemployment rate, a concern to all Newfoundlanders and Labradorians, and all Canadians and members of this House is falling from 18.2 per cent to 11 per cent. In our province, it has fallen a total of 10 per cent over that period of time.
We have seen in terms of growth and expansion in the economy 20 per cent, growth that the hon. member talks about as being unacceptable. In 1988, 223,000 homes were built in this country. In 1984, 135,000 homes were built in this country.
Let me talk more specifically, if I may, about the region. Total unemployment in Atlantic Canada has fallen by 33,000 compared to an increase of 65,000 between 1980 and 1984. In 1988, in Newfoundland and Labrador alone, we had the largest drop in unemployment of any province in this country and we saw an increase in jobs of 10,000, 10,000 people who were working that year but were not working the year before.
I have a short time left. I know my friend would like to comment. I do have one thing to say about unemployment insurance. Next year it is anticipated that $865
Supply
million in benefits will be paid into my province under employment insurance. The proposals made by this government will see a reduction of some $30 million out of $865 million in straight benefits.
We see an increase of $45 million for things like Community Futures, older workers, maternity benefits and benefits for those people who need help in times of sickness. Community Futures is a program which in my hon. friend's constituency has been shown to be hugely successful. In most of our provinces, it has been hugely successful and we have more money from this program.
The thing that aggravates me more than anything else when dealing with unemployment insurance is that narrow-minded, closed, "don't-change-anything" attitude. If we change nothing, we see no progress, we see no evolution, we see no hope. We must say to people that we keep adapting, we keep moving, we keep changing because there are options. This provides options.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to rise to congratulate my hon. friend from across the House on a first-class revelation of statistics. I do thank him for conceding that he enjoyed his visit to Bonavista-Trinity-Conception. I wonder if he would like to return and make that speech in the town hall that he just made. If he did, I would demand equal time. There are a number of things that I would like to say.
Statistics are a little bit like a lamp to a drunken sailor: more for support than for illumination. I would like to point out that what he did not mention was the money lost to UIC recipients in the province of Newfoundland alone. According to a reputable study-I cannot quibble with the figures-if we include the UI payments to recipients that they will not get plus the income tax benefits that would be paid anyway, the loss is $91.7 million. I have divided it three ways, and in the riding of Bonavista-Trinity-Conception, I cannot conceive of how to explain what $30 million means to my riding.
He also did not mention the very crucial area of job development that I deal with on almost an hourly basis in my riding. The hon. member knows that because he does the same thing. I am dealing with a loss of $53 million over all in the country and that affects me to a degree that causes me distress every day. I have to turn to people and say: "No, you cannot have your community hall, you cannot have your fire hall, you cannot have this

September 28, 1989
Supply
and you cannot have that," because all of a sudden the ground rules have changed.
The perception of Mr. de Grandpre, as I understand it, and I think we paid him $1.5 million to do this study, was a vision of a trampoline which would put you back into the training market and a safety net which was unemployment insurance if you fell off. The government wants to have the trampoline but not the safety net, so if you fall off the trampoline, you might go right through the safety net. That is what my people are concerned about. Mr. Speaker, I thank you for the opportunity to respond to my very learned friend.
Mr. Jack Shields (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister
for International Trade): Mr. Speaker, it gives me a great deal of pleasure to participate in the debate today. I would like to preface my remarks by pointing out what this government has done to restore Canada's competitiveness on international markets.
I would like to point out that we have done more in our term of office to improve our competitiveness in the international market-place than any other government in the history of this country. We have liberalized investment controls, we have deregulated energy and transportation, we have privatized many state-owned enterprises, we have developed a new labour market strategy, we concluded a free trade agreement with the United States and we have undertaken major reform of income and corporate taxes. We are now reforming our manufacturers' sales tax.
These moves have been and are part of a concerted plan to make markets function better for the benefit of all Canadians. Despite the inevitable transition problems that accompany major reforms, the longer term benefits are clearly apparent and have already done much to improve Canada's economic performance. There has been a remarkable rise in business investment in Canada over the past few years and that is testimony to the strong business confidence resulting from our policies.
Intended business capital spending in 1989 amounts to $82.7 billion. That is an increase of 13.6 per cent over 1988. That means jobs for Canadians. The OECD
projections of economic growth continue to put Canada ahead of the pack among member countries.
The next steps in improving our competitive position will involve measures to remove distortions in Canadian markets while securing our access to foreign ones. The new goods and services tax is an important instrument for that purpose.
The goods and services tax replaces a manufacturers' sales tax that has been universally recognized as obsolete and distortive. It is broken. In particular, replacing the manufacturers' sales tax with the GST removes the bias that exists, imports over domestic production that is there in the manufacturers' sales tax. Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, that we tax goods produced in Canada more than we tax goods being imported into Canada? We are shooting ourselves in the foot continuously every day that this manufacturers' sales tax stays in place.
The GST applies at a single rate of tax to a comprehensive base of traded goods and services leading to a more efficient allocation of resources. That helps to lower the cost of capital to Canadian businesses which makes them more competitive and it lessens the relative burden on manufacturers which makes the manufacturer more competitive.
Canada, as the Minister of Finance pointed out, joins an increasing number of industrialized countries that apply multi-stage consumption taxes. Those countries, it should be noted, have gained increased competition for their exports. It has done nothing but good for them. It has made them more competitive in the world market. Not least, implementation of this tax will remove a major source of uncertainty affecting growth and investment decisions.
Canada has for a long time been the only country to operate a sales tax at the manufacturing level and one that, by its very structure, disadvantages our own producers as compared to foreign exporters. That is why we have seen the influx of foreign goods at a more competitive price than Canadian goods on the shelves in our stores.
The manufacturers' sales tax taxes domestic inputs of marketing and distribution costs which were not fully captured in the tax levied on imports. Because the manufacturers' sales tax was essentially invisible from the point of the consumer, people were not aware of the effects on their choices as consumers. They did not know it was there. They did not know how much tax they were
September 28, 1989

paying on the goods that they purchased. It did not affect their choices as consumers or indeed their jobs as producers. The new goods and services tax will be visible and will remove or reduce the above biases to consumption and production.
In trade terms, Canada achieves by reform of the manufacturers' sales tax the removal of a self-inflicted wound. We are going to stop shooting ourselves in the foot. We increase the advantages to Canadian producers in markets in Canada and indeed when they export abroad, without, I might add, having to offer additional concessions to our trade partners.
The GST will lead to a significant improvement in the efficiency with which resources are allocated both within Canada and between Canada and other countries. The manufacturers' sales tax as it stands today provides for four different rates of tax. There are 22,000 special exemptions that have been won through the tax courts of Canada. Presently there are approximately 130 cases in the tax court seeking special exemption from the manufacturers' sales tax. Anyone with an ounce of sense would recognize that this distorts the relative prices of the commodities concerned and the investment choices that were made on that basis.
The reduced efficiency that flowed from this was reflected in output below potential. Canada's output today is below potential because of it. That reduces any gains that we might make from trade.
In contrast, the goods and services tax provides for a single rate of taxation applied to a comprehensive base of traded goods and services. The manufacturing sales tax incentive to shift out of manufacturing into services will be removed. Companies are restructuring, trying to move as much out of manufacturing into other areas of doing business and not always in a very efficient way. Producers, instead of concentrating on that kind of thing, will be able to allocate their productive capacity to the most economically remunerative purposes. That makes them more competitive.
This will be an important factor for the continuing restructuring of the Canadian economy to meet international competition. We must become internationally
Supply
competitive. Because Canada is a trading nation, our very prosperity depends on this competition.
With an efficient tax system, business can concentrate its efforts on decisions about the best use of real resources rather than concentrate on how to minimize tax liabilities. An efficient consumption tax will also serve to encourage savings, an element that is very important at a time of large demands for capital accumulation and restructuring of the economy.
This is a difficult period for many western economies. The stresses on international trade and payment systems have grown from a number of sources, escalating debt, weak commodity markets, major payment imbalances, proliferating terriers to trade. Canadian economic and trade policy has balanced the needs arising from these and other uncertainties in order to gain security and growth for Canadians.
Through the free trade agreement, we have secured duty-free access to the largest national market in the world. Access, however, will not do us any good if we do not also develop the competitive capabilities to make use of it and to extend our influence into other developed markets. This is what the GST will help us do together with other ongoing elements of the government's economic program.

I must say at the outset, Mr. Speaker, that the stoicism of my hon. friend from across the way is quite remarkable. The flames of protest against the GST are searing hot right across the country but particularly in his own home province of Alberta, and there he stands placidly, serenely, indifferently, as if nothing was going on outside of this House of Commons beyond Parliament Hill. It is as if the part of Canada where he lives belongs to some other planet. The fact of the matter is that Canadians are extremely upset about this tax and yet he did not recognize that fact at all in his 10 minute speech.
Since this government was first elected in 1984, it has failed to come to grips with the deficit despite all its protestations about the deficit. The debt has gone up from about $170 billion to $340 billion. This government has raised taxes not just 10 times, 20 times or 25 times but 30 times. I think the Leader of the Opposition identified the number of times this government has raised taxes: 31 times! Yet it is this government that talks

Supply
about its fiscal management as though it is doing such a tremendous job.
On top of this record of the past five years, now this government has the nerve, the unmitigated gall, to come along with this whopper called the GST and is going to gouge Canadian taxpayers to the tune of $10 billion extra as though we had just all kinds of money to throw away.
The Minister of Finance who spoke in this place just a few minutes ago has broken his promises over and over again on this issue. He talked about visibility of the tax. There is no visibility. He talked about a federal sales tax scheme that would be integrated with sales taxes in the provinces. Did that happen? No, it certainly did not. He has broken his promises over and over again.
He talked about the tax being revenue neutral. Some kind of revenue neutral. He admits or concedes that perhaps the additional gouging of taxpayers will go up to around $6 billion. We know it will be more than that. It will be closer to $10 billion.
I know I am running out of time, but I am coming to a question. Almost every major business group in this country is opposed to the GST. According to a CTV poll, 79 per cent of Canadians are against the GST and yet they push it through. I ask my hon. friend from across the way who shares one of the prairie provinces with me how in the name of heaven can this government justify pushing through this crushing tax?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would like to point out that I do not share Alberta with that hon. member.
The hon. member said that the province of Alberta was adamantly opposed to the imposition of the goods and services tax. That is true. It is because of the general type of rhetoric that we just heard from that hon. member when he stood up to ask a question. His rhetoric says that they will even tax your funeral.
I did not say that. It's true though.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
No, but I am telling you that that is the kind of rhetoric-it is true? Yes, that is true because right now we tax the shovel at 13.5 per cent, we tax the casket at 13.5 per cent, we tax the shroud at 13.5 per cent and we even tax the hearse at 13.5 per cent. After the GST is put in place, it will be 9 per cent, so who is being silly?
All they are doing is raising rhetoric. When they do that, I think they do a real disservice to Canadians in every walk of life. Hon. members, even if they are in opposition, should get hold of the facts and lay them out to the people instead of coming out with rhetoric that completely distorts. I might add that they are following the same tactic today that followed in the free trade debate. Look where it got them, right over there where they belong.

Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to be able to participate in this important debate today. It is an important debate because of the nature of the legislation pending. It is a very important debate because of the implications that this will have on the people of Canada.
Certainly the people of Canada have spoken loudly and the government has yet to listen. The goods and services tax is indeed a very bad tax. It is a tax that we have described as being in the wrong place at the wrong time. It is a tax which we discussed in Question Period and in previous speeches today as a tax which is just ludicrous to be imposing upon the people of Canada.
The motion before us today is one which I can support with a number of changes. The first part of the motion reads:
1) the threat to impose a new 9 per cent sales tax that is regressive, inequitable, invisible and inflationary;
While I agree with everything that is there, I would also agree with the motion if that had read 2 per cent, 1 per cent, 9 per cent, or 12 per cent. The number is irrelevant in this case. It is not a 9 per cent tax we are fighting, it is the tax we are fighting, the goods and service tax, the grief and suffering tax, as the hon. member for Kamloops said earlier.
In order to support some of the things that have been said around the country, the finance committee is looking to expand its hearings from the Ottawa area into the other cities of Canada. As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, the finance committee has decided that this is an important enough issue that it will extend the sittings to different places in Canada: Halifax, Edmonton, Vancouver. The closest that the finance committee will come to the area where I live in the constituency that I represent is the city of Regina.
September 28, 1989

My colleague in the provincial legislature, Doug Anguish, who formerly sat in this House and is now the MLA for The Battlefords, and I together are going to have our own public hearings in the city of North Battleford on October 7. We are going to listen to the concerns of the people of The Battlefords and The Battlefords-Meadow Lake constituencies because while the finance committee considers their views to be important, the finance committee cannot extend into all parts of Canada, particularly the rural and remote areas that are probably going to be affected harder by this tax than the urban parts of the country.
We want to give the people of our constituency the opportunity to present their views to the finance committee and to the Government of Canada. I have no doubt about some of the things I am going to hear when we hold our hearing in the city of North Battleford on October 7. The types of things I am going to hear will be similar to what has been provided to the finance Committee here in Ottawa and to us in the House of Commons by way of letters and the media.
A number of the things we are going to hear about are people in the retail sector expressing their frustration with the nature of the taxes that apply to their operations. First is the consumer end of it, having to fight on the front line, defending the collection of this tax to angiy consumers who are going to be paying this tax at the front end. It is not the finance minister who is going to have to stand there and explain why this box of diapers cost 9 per cent more today than it did yesterday. It is going to be a clerk or a store owner in small-town Saskatchewan who is going to have to say: "The government needs the money." It is not the finance minister who will hear that directly from the people who need those diapers and other services and goods that have not been taxed before at the retail level.
Certainly some things have not been taxed at all before. The hospitality industry, small hotels, cafes, gas stations, dry cleaning services, hair salons, in the smaller areas is suddenly going to be collecting a tax for the federal government because it is providing services to the people of its community. They become the tax collectors, and it is not these people over here or the
5,000	to 10,000 new tax collectors who are going to be hounding them who will actually be taking the money from the consumer. The small town, rural and remote business people are the ones who will have to take the
Supply
brunt of the frustration in the future for the strange moves of this government opposite.
I want to suggest a number of things. Earlier I had mentioned that it is not the 9 per cent but the tax of any per cent that I oppose. One of the things of which I am most scared is that this government, using the finance committee and parading witnesses in front of us, is going to try to provide a reason why, if 9 per cent is not appropriate, perhaps 6 per cent or 7 per cent will be appropriate.
We will have to broaden the base then because we still have to collect all of this extra money to pay off the deficit for the mismanagement of this government.
Seven per cent or 4 per cent attached to food now, this government tells us, will be acceptable to the Canadian people. Four years from now, that 4 per cent could become 9 per cent and it will be applied on food. We will not have gained anything by this debate and the frustrations expressed by people. All we will be doing by lowering the rates from 9 per cent to any other rate is simply forestalling the inevitable with these people on the other side of the House, and that is to have a broad based tax that is going to apply to food.
What does a broad based tax mean? We are just referring to it in terms of food, but what are the other exemptions? They are dental care, prescription drugs and those types of things that have been exempted. If we are broadening the base of this tax, we are talking about applying a tax to food, dental care and prescription drugs.
I, for one, want to be firmly on record, standing in this place, in front of all these people and anyone who is watching, as saying that I never want to see a tax on food, prescription drugs, medical appliances or heath care items of any kind at any time.
Why do we need all of this extra money? We are seeing ads from the government, and by the way, we cannot forget that the government has already indicated that it is prepared to spend $7 billion over the next two years to sell this tax to us through advertising. What is it that is causing this great need for this massive amount of money? It is not just the deficit. Do not forget that it is not that long ago that we stood in this chamber and debated the free trade legislation which was going to allow us to transfer and sell goods into the United States without tariffs. We argued then that that meant that we also would allow free access to the Canadian market for

September 28, 1989
Supply
American goods without tariffs. That move alone cost the Canadian people $2 billion in lost revenue.
Now the Canadian government is saying that we have lost the revenue and we have to make it up, let us charge the consumers, let us charge the poor, let us charge the people of Canada so that the Americans can sell cheaper goods on the Canadian market and take away Canadian jobs. I think that is an awful situation and it is one of the things that we have to keep in mind when we are dealing with this goods and services tax and the approach that this government is taking to all of us across the country.
There are a couple of other things that I want to express, particularly relating to agriculture. This government is pushing upon the farm community in Canada a whole broad range of exemptions for farm products under the goods and services tax. I do not want to play around with the nature of the tax at all and I do not agree that you put some things on and you provide exemptions on the end. The government is forcing farmers to pay cash up front, apply for rebates in the back and then expect that they will get paid back some time down the road. It is a ludicrous situation.
The point I want to make here is that if this government believes that the farm sector is important, then exempt the farm sector completely. Do not play around with this rebate and credit stuff. Exempt the farm sector if you consider it important and forget about the rebates, the delays and the cash flow problems that this whole situation is going to create for farmers, and that includes land transfers, leasing land, selling and transfer of crops and all of that sort of thing.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let me say to anybody who is thinking seriously about supporting the goods and services tax, think first about what it is that you want this tax to do. Is it to reduce the deficit? There are other ways to do that. Is it to make our trade better with the United States? There are other ways to do that. Is it to reform the Canadian tax system? There are other ways to do that and they are all much better. This goods and services tax does not address the needs of the Canadian economy. It addresses the needs of the government opposite and we have to change that. We have to do something about that. Unfortunately, for some of us it means waiting until the next election, but by golly we are
going to be there and the Canadian people are going to do that for us.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Clark (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have this opportunity to participate in this debate today, because certainly any debate relating to the economic policies of the government and hence the economic progress of the country is exceedingly important.
I think it is important to understand, when we look at the goods and services tax or any other particular part of the whole, that this government, going back to 1984, did in fact begin to develop and has put in place since then an over-all policy designed to generate the growth of a strong economy. I think what is important is to remember that each part of this policy has been part of an ongoing program. Naturally, we as citizens have a tendency to isolate the various proposals and to see them, perhaps, distinct from the other and to forget that indeed they are part of an ongoing policy. In doing that we may not fully appreciate the benefit of each.
This plan really had three central elements. First and foremost was the plan to reduce the deficit, because we understood as a government that unless we did something to reduce both the annual deficit and, eventually, the national debt, that we as a nation would indeed be crippled in the future. I think it is important to reiterate the fact that we have made good progress in the reduction of the annual deficit which must, of course, occur before we can reduce the debt itself. In fact, since 1984 the annual deficit has been reduced by $10 billion per year. I think that figure of $10 billion per year is worth repeating because there are a lot of people who forget that it exists.
In addition, it is also important to understand that in the plan, a part of which is now before the House of Commons, there is a further projected reduction in the annual deficit of $14 billion per year to be in place by 1993-1994.
We have also made good progress with respect to our proposals to permit Canada as a country to compete more effectively in the world market. Part of that, of course, is the free trade agreement which has been place for a few months and part of it also relates to the GATT talks which are an ongoing process and which are vital to
September 28, 1989

our future in light of the fact that we have been and will continue to be so heavily dependent on exports.
Third, as part of this plan, the government announced some time ago that it was exceedingly vital that we should have tax reform so that the policies of the government would be fair to all Canadians. It is this latter part of the over-all plan that I would like to speak about this afternoon, and to discuss where the GST fits in because it is, indeed, related to all three parts of the over-all plan.
Going back to November of 1984, Mr. Speaker, as you will recall, the government introduced what was called the Agenda for the Economic Renewal of Canada. That is when the government laid out its long-term plan describing how we would, over a period of time, put in place policies which would regenerate economic growth in this country. Within that policy framework there was emphasis on job creation, economic growth, sound fiscal management, economic efficiency and improved international competitiveness. Not only have we, as a government, followed this agenda with our economic policies, but I think we have real evidence that our plan is working. With our economic initiatives, from job creation and encouraging business investment to deregulation of energy and transportation sectors, our economic record begins to speak for itself.
The goods and services tax which by the way is a replacement tax, as I think all of us in this House understand but unfortunately which not all Canadians yet understand, is a continuation of that agenda, part of a plan to build a strong economy for Canada.
The 1987 White Paper on tax reform recommended that tax reform should take place in two phases. About a year ago we had phase one and today we are beginning the debate with respect to phase two. Briefly, as most of us understand, the goods and services tax which will be broadly based will replace a woefully inadequate and patently unfair 13.5 per cent manufacturers' sales tax which has been in place in this country since 1924.
I think it is important in passing to remind ourselves, and perhaps to remind Canadians, that every political
Supply
party in this House has agreed that the manufacturers' sales tax has been a disaster and that it must be replaced.
The evidence of its inefficiency and unfairness lies in the fact that of the 75,000 Canadian businesses which are part of the manufacturing sales tax some 22,000 have separate and independent tax arrangements. That, in itself, has to be evidence of unfairness and inefficiency.
We believe that the goods and services tax will benefit, once it is in place and once we understand it, Canadians in all regions. What I would like to talk about is how the goods and services tax will impact on farmers. That is also the subject of the discussion in which my hon. friend was participating.
Most of us understand that a number of items will be exempt from that tax. One is basic groceries. The fact that basic groceries will be tax free under the goods and service tax means that Canadians will not pay any tax whatsoever when they buy them. Making food-related products tax free will ensure that basic groceries are completely free of tax. With limited exceptions, almost everything sold by farmers, as a consequence, will be free of tax.
A farmer selling livestock or crops to a food processor will not charge a GST on that sale. Food processors will not charge a GST when they sell food-related agricultural products to the food wholesaler, and the wholesaler will not charge a tax when he sells products to the food retailer. In turn, of course, the retailer will not charge a tax when he sells products to the consumer.
The only products that will be taxed in this process when sold by farmers, and they are worth noting because they are relatively few in number, are cut flowers, trees, wood, bedding plants, sod, soil, bait, horses, unprocessed wool, fur, hides, seeds and natural fertilizer, except when sold in bulk.
Like other businesses, farmers will be able to claim the input tax credit on what they buy to use in their business. Since a farmer can claim back the tax which he pays on all of his business-related purchases, whether he is buying a tractor or paying for the services of a veterinarian, it is really to the advantage of the farmer, despite the fact that there w5ill be some more bookkeeping, to participate in the GST. I would note in passing that there will also be some very real economic gain to the farmer in certain specific instances which would come to mind. Take for example the purchase of a half-ton, which is so vital on the farms of western Canada and throughout the country. Assuming a $16,000 wholesale value for that

September 28, 1989
Supply
half-ton with a 13.5 per cent hidden manufactures' sales tax applied now, bearing in mind that tax will disappear and also that the farmer will receive a rebate on the 9 per cent goods and services tax paid on the retail price, he clearly comes out the winner, according to my mathematical calculations. On that $16,000 half-ton I think he would stand to gain some $2,160.
When he pays the telephone company for his service he will claim the tax back. Because the farmer has the option of reporting his purchases on a month-by-month basis he will virtually be in a position where there will always be tax owed to him. Therefore I do not believe, once the first two or three months are gone by, that the cash flow crisis about which some people have spoken will indeed be significant to that farmer. I would also remind the house that the farmer will also be in a position, should the rebates not be returned as quickly as he would wish, to receive interest on that after some 21 days.
The farmer is in a good position even when he sells his land because as long as he sells his land to an ongoing farm operation tax would not be applied. Even if it is sold in part the purchasing farmer would be eligible for the rebate. Should he sell his land to a developer, should it go from an agricultural to a non-agricultural use, the tax would apply, and I would suggest appropriately apply. If this is part of a transfer to part of the family there will not be a tax charge.
In conclusion, I think this tax will be good, once we understand it, for virtually all regions in Canada. It will be particularly good for western Canada because of our dependence on exports and I think it will be particularly well understood and well received by the farm community because the farm community in the end, I believe, will come out a winner.

Mr. Speaker, I had actually hoped to direct this protracted question to the hon. member for Athabasca, as he is a fellow Albertan, but any defender of the government's economic policies will do.
I rise, in fact, to support the motion of the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition and to ask a more general economic question of the hon. member, if I may, arising out, of the experience we in Alberta have had during the 1980s; two successive four-year terms, first of Liberals
and second of Tories federally, and of all Tories provincially from 1981 to 1988-89.
Let me start by quoting Statistics Canada employment earnings and hours to show you what the situation is now. In March, 1989, the average hourly- paid employee in the goods producing sector in Alberta worked 37.8 hours a week for an hourly rate of $14.80. By contrast, the average hourly-paid employee in the service sector worked 28.4 hours a week for an average hourly wage of $10.37 an hour: At the lower end of the service sector are trade, finance, insurance and real estate, and at the very lowest end are those jobs associated with tourism with a rate of pay of less than $6.50 an hour, for an average of just over 26 hours per week and a gross pay of about $172 a week. That is the current employment situation in Alberta.
What we find is that between 1981 and 1988 in Alberta employment in the goods producing sector actually fell from about 403,000 to about 342,000, a decrease of 15 per cent. Meanwhile employment in the service sector grew from about 748,000 to 845,000, an increase of about 13 per cent. The largest increase was in the services subsector, that poorer subsector, which grew from about
322.000	to about 402,000, an increase of almost 25 per cent. At the same time, the highest unemployment was experienced in the services producing industries, about 61 per cent of all unemployed in Canada, as a matter of fact.
This parallels a growth in part-time work. In 1988,
184.000	or 15.5 per cent of all jobs in Alberta were classified as part time, a growth of about 39,000 from 1981. During this same eight-year period full-time employment actually fell from 1,007,000 to 1,003,000, a decrease of about 0.4 per cent while officially recognized part-time employment increased by 27 per cent.
Successive Liberal and Conservative Governments have seen employment in full-time jobs fall, in part-time jobs rise, in well-paying jobs fall, in poor-paying jobs rise. I ask the hon. member is this the success of which he boasts?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have a member from Alberta ask a question, particularly bearing in mind the fact that I think the whole question of the goods and services tax in Alberta is of particular interest to the people of that province because most of them seem to not understand that indeed they have been paying the manufacturers' sales tax and that they are part of a tax-paying public whether they have been paying a direct provincial sales tax or not.
September 28, 1989

So there is a 13.5 per cent tax that has been applied throughout Alberta and because it is hidden there has not been any accountability for that.
Without being able to comment specifically on the statistics which the hon. member has cited relating to his province, I would like to say a few words. First, with respect to the million and a half jobs that have been created since 1984 in this country, I do know that 80 per cent of them are full-time jobs, which was in fact a contrast with the situation as it was before 1984.1 find it hard to believe that that pattern would vary substantially in one part of the country from that which exists elsewhere. I think that 80 per cent full-time jobs across the country is a very important accomplishment.
I would also suggest to the hon. member that his province, like so many provinces, has been very dependent upon one or two parts of an economy. Certainly the agricultural economy has had difficulties in the last three or four years, mostly difficulties created by climate over which we have little or no control. However, I would say to. this member, as one who is very proud of what we have done in agriculture, that this party, this government, has done more to assist Alberta farmers and farmers in every other part of the country than has any other government in the history of this country.
I would also suggest to the hon. member that part of the difficulties in the Alberta economy relate very much to what has been happening in oil. If I recall correctly, his party, if not himself, because he was not here, was a very strong supporter of the National Energy Program which those two parties across the way put in place. It had a tremendous negative impact on the economy of Alberta.
I think you will see, Mr. Speaker, that certainly the goods and services tax will help Alberta because of its dependence on exports, because the manufacturers' sales tax in place now discriminates against manufacturing in Canada. It also has made it very difficult for us to export abroad because the manufacturers' sales tax has been included in the price of those goods sold elsewhere. The goods and services tax will not be charged on products being exported outside the country. That will
Supply
help the province of Alberta. That will help all of western Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I want to take part in the debate today because I believe that no country can have a strong economy to carry it through the turn of the century unless it follows a sound fiscal policy. This Conservative Government has totally missed the boat in the past two years. Everybody in Canada-employers, trade unions, ordinary people and major corporations alike-agreed on the fact that a real tax reform was needed. But the Government put it off, changed its mind and, as we recall, in the fall of 1984 and in the spring of 1985 the Minister of Finance told us there was no point in revamping the tax system because everything was forever changing. So all that was needed were small corrective measures to take prevailing conditions into account. But the minute he realized that the United States would be coming up with their own tax reform he decided we had to have one as well.
Even then everybody agreed we had to reform the system. So the Minister, ever mindful of the upcoming election, chose to bring in the tax reform in two stages: first stage, the income tax, second stage, the sales tax reform. I remember very well that when the Committee on Finance began studying the first stage most witnesses before the committee said we were making a mistake and that the two stages should have been considered at the same time because a sound fiscal policy has to include income and sales or consumer taxes, both fully harmonized as a whole to achieve economic recovery.
But as I said, for electoral considerations, he did the opposite and we are now looking at a tax reform, an income tax reform which does not really meet our requirements. And today here we are dealing with a sales tax refom which Canadians reject outright. We have heard about a number of polls. A couple of days ago, I think, one such poll revealed that 78 per cent of Canadians are against the TGS, the tax on goods and services. Amopg others, the Canadian Federation of Independent Business reported that 97 per cent of small businesses completely reject this tax.

Supply
Well, the Minister of Finance may have the impression that he got through the first stage before the election by allowing the odd income tax rate reduction and that we are now prepared to swallow the second stage right after the election. If he thinks that Canadians will forget all about it between now and the next time they vote, Mr. Speaker, I would suggest he and the Prime Minister are mistaken because Canadians are not about to forget. People throughout the country are now getting organized to set off a real tax revolt. Canadians find this tax unacceptable.
Given what little time I have left, I should like to deal more particularly with small business. Just what does this tax mean to small business? It will be a total nightmare, Mr. Speaker. We now have close to 900,000 small businesses in Canada and out of these 900,000 businesses perhaps a small percentage is affected by the existing federal sales tax.
So all small businesses! And the Minister in his technical paper proposes that businesses with sales of $30,000 a year will not be affected, will not have to register for the sales tax, the new goods and services tax. Mr. Speaker, I think that is really a joke. Think of what $30,000 is worth today and what it will be worth in 1991.
So in fact all small businesses will register for this tax and we have reason to believe that the 4,000 public servants-and I do mean four thousand, Mr. Speaker- whom the Department of Revenue will employ just to administer this tax will not be sufficient.
Imagine the anxiety of Canadian small business people now, because they do not really know what to expect; it is complex.
An item may be taxable or it may not be. The new system the Minister is proposing to us will make items taxable not according to what they are but depending on the establishment and the origin of the establishment.
Mr. Speaker, imagine the complexity. Big business, banks and big corporations will not have problems because they have management systems, fairly sophisticated accounting systems that will enable them to carry on.
The Minister defends himself, as we saw yesterday when he tried to answer my question, by saying they have provided two simplified accounting systems.
With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say what John Bullock, president of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, thinks about these two simplified systems.
I am quoting John Bullock, president of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business. He said that nevertheless, the simplified accounting methods proposed by the Government are even more complex than the rest of the system.
He said that on September 9 in The Ottawa Citizen. So much for simplicity, Mr. Speaker. We know very well from Mr. Bullock's testimony that the extra administrative costs for Canadian small businesses will be from $1,000 to $3,000, depending on the additional equipment they will have to buy, a new cash register or whatever.
Mr. Speaker^ the $600 the federal Government proposes to compensate small businesses is not adequate and several witnesses have asked that this amount be increased.
During the past five years in the House, Members, and especially Government Members, constantly said how pleased and proud they were of small businesses which generated between 80 and 85 per cent of our employment. I am also proud of these small businesses, Mr. Speaker, and I have always been a staunch defender of small business. Today, however, these people are afraid. Canadians who would like to start a new business are now afraid to do so, because of this nightmare of a new tax, the GST. Jobs that would otherwise have been created will not materialize.
Last night, Mr. Speaker, we heard that apparently, Canada's tourism industry will lose at least 30,000 jobs. Mr. Speaker, 30,000 jobs will be lost because of this new tax!
When people say that the old tax-

Like the Minister used to say and still says in his speeches, "this federal manufacturers' sales tax is a killer of jobs". Well we find out that the new GST, goods and services tax, is also a killer of jobs. So what are we doing here? We are changing four quarters for a dollar and are making all Canadians miserable. New small businesses will not be created because of fear. People will say: "Why should I invest my money? Why should I risk my shirt? Why should I risk everything I worked for all my life
September 28, 1989

when maybe a few years hence a tax inspector will walk into my business and say, 'you did not charge the tax right.'" He does not know what is taxable and what is not taxable. The businessman is going to be asked to pay the tax, the penalty and the interest and he will lose everything he has worked for all his life. That is the kind of business attitude we are creating in this country.
If we say that small business is the backbone of our economy then we should stop this madness and the minister should withdraw this project immediately. He should go to the provinces, negotiate, and have one tax system in this country once and for all so that everyone can understand and we can have some business activity that makes sense.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Resuming debate. The Hon. Member for Richmond-Wolfe (Mr. Cote).

Mr. Speaker, sales tax reform is essential, as I see it, and is part of the Government's plan to provide for a better economic future for Canada.
One of the major obstacles to achieving this objective is our increasing national debt.
Before discussing the goods and services tax the GST and how it works, I would like to talk about our national debt.
Everyone agrees that this debt is a national problem. Controlling the debt is a challenge that is national as well, and what we need is a national commitment, if we are to meet this challenge and overcome this obstacle.
Borrowing money, having debts is not necessarily a bad thing. If I want to buy a house, I have to borrow. Borrowing is, in itself, dynamic. It is not necessarily risky as long as we are able to meet our monthly payments.
Ongoing debt, however, is a problem. If I am unable to meet my monthly payments on the house I just bought, I go into debt. If I borrow money to buy more goods, I accumulate more debt which I cannot repay and I end up with my back against the wall.
Supply
Being in debt is a problem. It has been Canada's problem for the last 25 years, and a problem for private individuals and businesses as well.
When your debts are too high and interest payments are high as well, then the situation becomes extremely difficult.
Public debt has existed since the beginning of Confederation, but it was not until the past 20 or 25 years that our debt took on astronomical proportions.
Since 1970-1971, the federal Government has spent annually more than it receives in revenue. This takes us back to the monthly mortgage payments I am unable to meet on my house. Those missed payments become a debt.
Briefly, the Government has had an ongoing deficit since that time. In order to deal with these deficits, we and our successive predecessors had to borrow. The cumulative result of all this borrowing has become what is referred to as the national debt, which today totals $320 billion.
Imagine what this means in interest payments alone! Thirty-one cents of every dollar of revenue received by the Government is used to service the debt.
Last year, interest payments alone represented $1,300 per Canadian citizen. Men, women and even children were in debt. This means average of $5,000 per family or $400 per individual, per month, the equivalent of a very substantial proportion of the rent or mortgage payments we all have to pay. This cannot go on. We are now with our backs against the wall. But in order to reduce the debt to a manageable level, we have to reduce the annual deficit. That is exactly what we have done since 1984.
At that time, in 1984, the deficit was $38.3 billion. Just for the fiscal year ending in March 1989, provisional data show the deficit was $28.7 billion, which is $200 million less than forecast in the April budget projections. So we have reduced the deficit by some $9.5 billion from the 1984 level. That means that every year, we have reduced our expenditures by $10 billion, maybe not to spend on the extra services we would like, because there is always the total debt to consider, but we have already reduced the deficit, which stood at $38 billion, by $10 billion.

September 28, 1989
Supply
This deficit reduction has thus slowed the growth of the public debt. In the last fiscal year, for the first time in 15 years-yes, fifteen years-the debt increased by less than 10 per cent. That is a good performance, compared to the peak of 24 per cent growth in 1984.
But our objective is to reduce our borrowing requirements to zero by 1993-94, and that is a major challenge. It means wiping out the whole $28 billion deficit we still have. Using the same accounting methods as the United States and Great Britain, we would then have what is called a balanced budget.
Our overall success with deficit reduction since 1984 is due to tighter control on all expenses in all areas. First, we cut public expenditures. Second, we overhauled the whole tax system. Finally, we made structural changes to help the economy function more harmoniously and productively, without too much government interference.
Expenditure restraint, Mr. Speaker, was and is a major part of our debt control program. I heard people say, not only today but for several weeks, that if the government reduced its expenditures, they would not be so unhappy about paying taxes. Well and good. Everyone is for cutting expenditures instead of raising taxes. But in fact, that is just what we have done, restrict and decrease government expenditures, not just a little, but a lot.
Let's take a closer look. Consider what has happened. We made cuts in every area of public spending. A lot of people say: Make cuts in the public service. Cut property. Cut buildings. Don't forget we reduced grants to businesses, like incentives for the petroleum industry. We also cut funding for Crown corporations, including The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and Canada Post. We did that. We also reduced spending on defence and foreign aid. A lot of people are criticizing us for this. So where should we cut? We had to do something. We also made changes in our programs for income transfers to individuals. People on high incomes now have to return part of their old age security pension and family allowance. The list of cutbacks does not end there, and it will continue to grow. In fact, many of these decisions were extremely difficult to make. But they were necessary, and we made those decisions. In fact, it is all part of a government's responsibility to manage the well-being of the entire community. Of course, this requires sacrifices
on the part of certain sectors of the population, but this Government has shown in the past four years that it is able to act responsibly.
Spending cutbacks have been very visible in government operations. Last year, spending on government operations was less than it was when we took power. In four years have we cut government spending to a level even lower than it was four years ago. What a performance!
We managed to do so by imposing severe budgetary constraints on the departments. We sold surplus public property. We cut the Public Service by 12,000 person-years. There again, people are saying: Cut, cut! However, we cannot keep on cutting. We must maintain our services and the people who manage them. Nevertheless, we managed to cut 12,000 person-years. We spent $1.7 billion on government operations last year 10 per cent less compared with 1984-85. Many businesses would be delighted with those results. And we are determined to continue to identify and deal with any instances of taxpayers' money being wasted.
We have been able to keep program spending increases down to an average of only 3.5 per cent annually, since we came to power. This increase is less than the inflation rate for the same period. Last year-an election year-we kept increases in program spending down to 3.1 per cent. In comparison, spending by provincial governments increased 6.5 per cent. Once again, what a performance!
These measures, Mr. Speaker, made it possible to reduce program spending from 19.5 per cent in 1984-85 to 16 per cent, in terms of last year's gross domestic product. Further reductions will be achieved this year and in the years to come. Without our budgetary restraint measures, program spending this year would have been $22 billion more than it is today.
When we look at the deficit, we must consider the spending aspect and, of course, taxes. Nobody likes taxes. Nobody wants to pay taxes. But even if we don't like taxes, we know we have to pay them, and that is how we should approach the proposed goods and services tax.
The first stage of tax reform was done with this in mind. The second stage is the one we are talking about today. Canadians must understand, Mr. Speaker, that government is a service that must be paid for. Of course, the Opposition tends to be alarmist in its statements, but
September 28, 1989

I think, Mr. Speaker, we should point to all the information that has been made available.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for my colleague the Hon. Member for Richmond-Wolfe (Mr. Cote). It is not a matter of being alarmist, Mr. Speaker, it is a matter of fact. I happen to know that we in Canada have certain taxation problems. Corrective steps must be taken. I would think everybody in the House is aware of that. But, Mr. Speaker, what has me seriously concerned about the TGS announced by the Conservative Government is that 75 per cent of Canadians have indicated in no uncertain terms that they are against this tax on goods and services, and what has me even more worried, Mr. Speaker, is that Quebec is one of the provinces which will be hardest hit by the 9 per cent tax on goods and services. So here is my question to the Member for Richmond-Wolfe.
You in the Conservative Government have always sought to reach a consensus with the Canadian provinces, so how is it that in this case, barely a few weeks ago at the federal-provincial conference held in Quebec City, all Canadian premiers unanimously spoke against the tax on goods and services? Yet the Canadian provincial premiers are your partners and you have to try to reach a consensus with the provinces concerning provincial or federal tax issues. So I would like to know what our colleague thinks. Since everybody is against it, can the Government not realize it is taking the wrong approach with respect to the kind of tax it wants to impose on Canadians?

I am amazed Mr. Speaker that the Hon. Member's assessment of the situation is that of a total opposition. If he was attending the hearings or reading the submissions, he would realize that everyone of those who have appeared up till now supports the principle of the GST, because it is a fair and equitable alternative to another tax, the manufacturers' sales tax, which indeed was unfair. What you should know is that all the witnesses are suggesting to the Government through the Committee, of course to perhaps propose alternative implementation mechanisms than those tabled in a working paper which indeed we are discussing.

When you also suggest that there is no unanimity among the provinces, I can indicate that if there is no unanimity between themselves, there is no lack of it as far as discussions with the Canadian Government are concerned. There is rather more unanimity between provinces, but as to that the discussions are continuing.
The third matter raised by the Hon. Member, Mr. Speaker, is that alarmist sentiment. And I must submit that the Hon. Member used the right word because the discussions that are now going on are alarmist indeed to the extent those fears are expressed by the Opposition. It is clear people oppose this if the surveys you are referring are to be believed. But as I said to the extent the discussion is proceeding in a cold, dispassionate manner, my appreciation is altogether different and witnesses appearing before the Committee have very supportive views indeed.

Mr. Speaker, I rise in this debate to talk about browbeating. I would like you to give me some latitude, Mr. Speaker, because I believe this is relative to the goods and services tax that the government plans to introduce.
I would like to read an editorial from the Winnipeg Free Press. It is entitled: "Browbeating Newfoundland".
The Prime Minister last week sent one of his top underlings to tell a press briefing that Newfoundland's second thoughts could threaten not only the Meech Lake Accord but all federal-provincial agreements and, indeed, the very international order. If Newfoundland could change its mind about Meech Lake, he warned, no agreement between governments could stand. The federal-provincial agreement to develop the Hibernia oilfield off the shores of Newfoundland would be at risk; so could fisheries agreements with the United States.
This was an unprecedented move by a senior official of the Government of Canada warning Newfoundland, saying to Newfoundland: "You be careful or otherwise you're going to be cut off." I have never seen such shameless intimidation in the 17 years that I have been in the House of Commons.
I want to tell the members of the House of Commons the context for this intimidation. This is a province that has been warned to behave itself, a province which has already suffered immensely, immeasurably, at the hands of this government. It is a province, first of all, that has seen its fish stock, its very lifeblood, threatened. The crisis that we see in the east coast fishery now is unprecedented. And we began as a fishing province, Mr. Speaker. That is what we are all about. That is what our

people do. That is why they are there in the first place. Those people who say: "Why don't you do something else?" really don't understand the situation at home. Our people fish, and yet the fish stocks are in crisis as a result of the mismanagement of the Government of Canada. They are the government; they bear the responsibility.
In the midst of this crisis on our very doorsteps, at the heart of our very livelihood, the Government of Canada says: "At this time, Newfoundland, Labrador, we intend to change the unemployment insurance system in this country" which is the safety net that fishermen and plant workers have used as an income support program since the days of Jack Pickersgill.
At the time the fishery, the main industry, is in crisis, the Government of Canada says: "We're increasing your premiums. We're withdrawing from the unemployment insurance plan. We're cutting back on the number of weeks of benefit you can draw. That's what we're going to do for you in a time of crisis." There is no compensation plan, as was provided for the farmers of Canada. There is no plan for managing the stocks. They are cutting back on the safety net on the unemployment insurance plan which is the safety net for plant workers in Newfoundland. That is number two.
The third thing the Government of Canada did was to short change the east coast in terms of regional development. I want to read from The Ottawa Citizen of September 13. This is a study commissioned by the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council-not a Tory rag, not a Liberal organization, not an NDP organization. It is the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council. Do you know who did the study for them? Decima did the study for them, the polling agency of the Tory party. The polling agency of the Prime Minister did a survey for the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council and here is what they found:
-federal industrial assistance to the Atlantic provinces has fallen to such an extent that in 1987 it was, per capita, below the national average.
Let me repeat that for the record. It is important. This is a Decima survey.
-federal industrial assistance to the Atlantic provinces-
Remember regional development? Remember DREE? Remember co-operative federalism? Remember a kind Canada, a sharing nation? Remember reaching out to the underprivileged and the underdog and those who had less? Remember that? Here is what Decima says:
-federal industrial assistance to the Atlantic provinces has fallen to such an extent that in 1987 it was, per capita, below the national average-
The business-funded economic research council found that federal assistance to Atlantic Canada amounted to $1,045 per person.
That compared to $229 per person in the rest of Canada and $302 per person for all of Canada.
I have not got time to dwell on that point, but it is point number three.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I would also like to talk about western diversification and what we are doing in Atlantic Canada under ACOA as well as FEDNOR with the head office in Sault Ste. Marie.
On August 4, 1987, the government announced a major new initiative to bring the west more fully into the mainstream of national economic development, ready to respond to the changing global economic realities. Much has been done in the two years to achieve that aim.
Despite the present period of fiscal restraint, the national challenge has been to reduce the federal deficit. We are working to continue with even more energy-wise ideas and more commitments into our regional areas to make sure that they receive not just the same amount of funding as last year but, indeed, increased funding.
Western diversification has been increasing its spending. In 1987-1988 our cash outlay was $52 million. In 1988-1989 this increased to $145 million. For the 1989-90 fiscal year our Main Estimates show $287 million. Compared to actual expenditures last year, the Main Estimates tabled in 1989 provide for a $142 million increase. That is a $142 million increase for western diversification.
September 28, 1989

Funding expectations have been very high, and in a period of fiscal restraint, not all expectations can be met, nor should all of them be met. But the government remains highly committed, as these increases for expenditures show, to major regional development, especially efforts in the west and in our eastern regions in Atlantic Canada.
The government established the Department of Western Economic Diversification in response to special needs of western Canadians. This government recognized that the economic challenges of each region of this country differ and that a new and innovative way of dealing with economic development was needed. Western Diversification and ACOA reflect this new approach.
To ensure success Western Diversification's mandate was kept simple with three main objectives: First, to provide responsible leadership for economic development in the west; second, to undertake a strong advocacy role in order to represent western Canadian views in decision-making process here in Canada; and, third, to use widely accepted business principles in establishing a program in support of diversification. The act was passed and proclaimed on June 25, 1988.
WD has taken on a new task and its officials keep plugged in to interdepartmental policy processes here. They keep plugged in to the day-to-day processes of the government in order to ensure that the interests of western Canadians are fully considered here in Ottawa and are listened to very clearly in our offices across the west.
Western interests are also being pursued with the cabinet in a number of key areas. The main one I want to talk about is the procurement and development of national resource policies.
The Western Procurement Initiative, WPI, which was announced in July, 1988, was a specific move for western Canada. First, increasing the level of high value added. Second, discretionary procurement funding to be sourced in the west by an increment of $600 million over four years has been set aside. Third, making best efforts to designate significant portions of major Crown projects for sourcing in the west, and only in the west. Fourth, putting the full weight of the Western Diversification fund behind efforts to pre-position western suppliers so that they may be better prepared to compete for public
Supply
sector contracts. Fourth, working with provincial governments to ensure an effective network is being put behind a supplier and in the pre-positioning of suppliers to bid on government procurement contracts.
Presently, a procurement memorandum of understanding is being drawn up with the Departments of National Defence, Supply and Services, Industry, Science and Technology, and the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency.
Western Diversification works with other departments. For example, it works and shares with Agriculture Canada on biotechnology and in soil conservation; with Energy, Mines and Resources on clean, low sulphur coal.
To be eligible for WD assistance, projects have to relate to new products, new markets, new technologies, increases in productivity or import replacements. Western diversification supports both individual commercial projects and systemic projects. We do not take an equity position at all. speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened very attentively to the discourse of our colleague across the way and I want to ask her a question.
The hon. member spoke of regional development and of other interesting issues. More specifically, I want to know whether she is in favour of the goods and services tax, first, as is presently proposed by the Minister of Finance. Second, I want to ask her about the following: The Minister of Finance said today that the goods and services tax was a component of the government's program to lower the deficit.
Given that the Minister of Finance said on June 18, 1987 that this tax would be revenue neutral, I wonder whether my colleague can tell me how a revenue neutral tax can possibly reduce the deficit.

Mr. Speaker, I was just opening the technical book on the goods and services tax. I do believe my colleague's first question had to do with whether I was in favour of the proposed goods and services tax.
I guess you have to understand where we are coming from and maybe it takes time to explain that what we have in place, the federal sales tax, or the manufacturing sales tax, was initiated in 1924 when 85 per cent of the employment was in the manufacturing industries here in Canada and actually less than 10 per cent, probably about 8.5 per cent employment was in the service industry.
Life has changed as obviously we have evolved over the last six decades and we are now in an era where over 70 per cent or 75 per cent of the people in Canada are employed in the service industry rather than what I would call the manufacturing industry or the resource industry. So that has changed completely.
In 1924 there was a tax applied on manufactured goods only, and that was applicable at that time. But today life has changed and we have a average 13.5 per cent tax applied to the manufacturing industry. This is not fair. This is why our Minister of Finance is moving to broaden the base and to bring in other industries and services so that we are all treated equally, and it is an equitable position. Yes, I am in favour of a goods and services tax,

but we have to have a package. If we want to have certain exemptions, basic foods, health care costs, certain dental care services, municipalities, universities, schools, hospitals, and certain legal fees exempted, and so they should be, then we need a 9 per cent tax.
The Minister of Finance must have a 5.5 per cent rate if he is to obtain $18.5 billion which is raised today from the old, archaic, obsolete tax. We have to have the $18.5 billion.
The Minister of Finance is going to implement a goods and services tax credit that will assist lower income Canadians. He is going to lower the rate of tax from 26 per cent to 25 per cent for middle income Canadians. This is stated in his technical papers. If he is to have this, and if he is to have the exemptions, it works out to the 9 per cent. Therefore, if you want to lower the rate, you have to broaden the base.
The second question my colleague asked was with regard to revenue neutral. Certainly, this has been discussed quite a bit recently and I do believe some months ago the minister did mention revenue neutral.
The tax that we have today which raises the $18.5 billion has 22,000 exceptions and has hundreds of people who avoid or get out of paying the tax. There are many manufacturing companies that during their process stage would do one value-added here, and then through a subsidiary they would pass off the value-added product into another company and therefore avoid the tax. This is happening. No one, not your government when you were in power, Sir, nor this government, knows exactly how many companies are either avoiding or getting out of paying the tax. We do not know how many people we are missing out there. Hopefully, if we are missing a lot it will perhaps gain us more revenue than what the Minister of Finance said. However, if you look at the technical papers, and at the diagrams which the Minister of Finance has put in them,he shows exactly what he needs to replace the $18.5 billion, what he needs to have the goods and sales tax credit for the lower income people, what he needs to have in order to have the rate drop from 26 per cent to 25 per cent for the middle income people, and what he needs, which is the $.2 billion, for the administrative costs.
