Mr. Speaker, I rise today to pursue a question that I asked of the Prime Minister before the summer break actually but a question which is still very current. In fact, I had the opportunity to ask a question about the same thing today, namely, the proposed cuts to VIA Rail passenger rail service in Canada and, in particular, the way in which the environmental dimension of this decision has been ignored by the government.
On the same day that I asked the question in June, the Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan asked the Prime Minister whether or not an environmental assessment had been done of the proposal to cut back severely on passenger rail service in Canada. The Prime Minister rose in his place and said that it was a budgetary decision and that budgetary decisions are not normally subjected to environmental assessment, thus giving the lie to all that has been said in the last many months since the Brundtland Commission report came out about the extent to which this government was taking seriously the recommendations of that commission, that all major economic decisions should be assessed for their environmental impact. Surely a decision to cut a couple of hundred million dollars from the annual subsidy to VIA Rail, and knowing that the consequence would be a significant reduction in passenger rail service, qualifies as a major economic decision.
All we are saying to the government is that if you want to be true to your own rhetoric, if you want to be true to your own commitments, if you want to demonstrate that you really have entered into this new way of thinking about the economy and this new way of thinking about the relationship between economic and environmental matter, then here is the perfect opportunity. Here is the perfect opportunity to say that the world has changed, our way of thinking about the economy has changed and our way of thinking about federal expenditures has changed and before we make any decisions with respect to VIA Rail, this time and for the first time, we will take into account the environmental externalities of passenger rail service, those things which are normally not accounted for in the regular way we do our bookkeeping vis-a-vis passenger rail service.
We have made that kind of argument before just on the subsidy level. All the subsidies to passenger rail, or for that matter rail period, are all up front, they are all in the railway's books. But the subsidies to airports, to highways, to automobile use and to buses are all hidden subsidies that are kept in a different set of books. That is one argument.
An even further argument is that there is a whole other set of books with respect to the priority of one way of transporting people over another. That has to do with the environment and it has to do with safety. We know that in many parts of Canada the highways are already too crowded. We know that in some parts it is due to deregulation and the increase of truck traffic over rail traffic. We know that there is still a tremendous rate of death on the highways as a result of this overcrowding but also as a result of a way of life centred around the automobile.
In terms of deaths caused by various modes of transportation, I remember the derailment in Hinton. We have a Hinton a week on the highways and yet no one seems to take that into account. That is one thing that should be taken into account. We ought not to make that situation worse, yet that is what the government proposes to do.
September 28, 1989

Second, with respect to the environment, the government and its spokesmen, the Prime Minister and others, go all around the globe addressing problems. We have to reduce our use of hydrocarbons, we have to stem the greenhouse effect. We have to deal with the question of low-level ozone which has to do with exhaust emissions, not high level ozone and the depletion thereof but low level ozone at ground level. There are all these increasing global environmental problems that are related to over-use of the automobile. It is as simple as that.
Yet what do we have? Instead of a government that is really trying to address that, that is trying to make some of the difficult decisions, we have the Minister of Transport get up today and say that this is costing a lot of money. Well, it will not only cost money, it will cost us our survival as a human race if we do not start to make these kinds of decisions differently.
The Canadian people have said in a variety of ways, not just through the polls, but through the support that they have given to people who are concerned about the environment that they are willing to support policies, even expensive policies, if those policies tend toward an environmentally sustainable future. People are willing to pay for that. They are not willing to pay for the GST and I do not blame them. I would venture to guess they would be willing to pay some form of even higher taxes if they thought that they were going to be directed toward a transportation system that did not pollute or toward other environmentally sound policies.
I think the government is really missing an opportunity to show leadership here. The minister says only 3 per cent use passenger rail service. The minister cannot possibly be that stupid. I challenge the minister to try to get a seat on many of the trains that he proposes to cut.
I had an opportunity to travel on the train a couple of times this summer and I was on a train on which I could not get a seat. Yet the Minister has the nerve to say that people are not using the trains. Well, there are people who are not using the trains because they cannot get a spot on the trains, the trains are so full.
If you want to get a sleeper from Winnipeg to Vancouver next summer, you had better book now. It
Adjournment Debate
might not do you any good now, thanks to the proposal of the government, but people are having to book way ahead of time. Why? Because the trains are getting shorter and shorter. Why are the trains getting shorter and shorter? Because there is less and less equipment. Why is there less and less equipment? Because there is no investment. Why is there no investment? Because the Conservatives do not keep their promises.
There is a wonderful opportunity lost for the environment, for Canada and even for this government to show just once it was not kidding western Canadians when it paraded itself around western Canada saying that it would be the great saviour of VIA Rail. It lied, and that is the most despicable element of this, more than anything else.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Belsher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there were times, while the member was speaking, when I was wondering whether he was talking about the same question as the one he had asked a few months back in this House, but then he finally got around to the environment.
It is a misconception in Canada that trains are the most efficient mode of passenger transportation. Energy efficiency depends to a large extent on passenger levels. VIA, with its generally low occupancy rates is not nearly as energy efficient as is often assumed.
In 1980, a study on energy consumption concluded that buses, not trains, were the most energy efficient mode of transport in Canada based on energy consumed per passenger mile. Eighty-four per cent of all intercity travel is by car, 6 per cent is by bus, and only 3 per cent is done by train.
Emissions from automobiles and buses have dropped by 75 per cent since the early 1970s. In an effort to further reduce these emissions, the Ministers of the Environment and of Transport Canada recently announced a joint action plan to put in place within five years the most stringent regulations that technology will allow to control emissions from internal combustion engines that bum fossil fuels.
This tough new controls package could further reduce by up to 30 per cent emissions of nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds which contribute to smog and to acid rain. It could also cap carbon dioxide

September 28, 1989
Adjournment Debate
emissions which cause global warming and will reduce toxics produced by the use of motor fuels.
Federal assessments of environmental and health benefits, associated economic impacts and technological feasibility will be completed within 24 months. Regulatory proposals will begin to be published within 36 months and regulations could become effective within 48 months. Standards established in 1987 and 1988 under the Motor Vehicle Safety Act will effectively lower air pollution from on-road vehicles over the next decade.
Given the above and the small amount of intercity rail travel, any shift in rail passengers to buses or the automobile should therefore have a minimal environmental impact.

Mr. Speaker, on September 261 put a question to the Minister of Agriculture asking him why the government misled the Canadian dairy industry in the spring of 1988 when the Minister of Agriculture told Canadian dairy farmers that they would preserve the underpinnings of the supply management and marketing board system in this country by simply moving ice cream and yogurt and other dairy products from the tariff list to the import control list, that tariffs were coming off because of the free trade deal.
The minister said very clearly that he would preserve the underpinning of the supply management and marketing board system by simply putting these products over so that there will not be a flood of cheap surplus processed dairy products coming in from the United States. He led Canadian dairy farmers to believe that there was some arrangement with the Americans under the free trade deal, that there would not be this challenge, that there would not be a flood of these dairy commodities coming into Canada.
It was a given that under the 1955 waiver the Americans have from GATT their market was closed to our dairy producers for these commodities going into the United States. But clearly the minister, on many occasions in the House of Commons and otherwise, led Canadian farmers to believe that the import controls on these items would be protected the underpinning for the supply management system.
On June 13, 1988, in the House of Commons, in responding to a question from the Leader of the Opposition, he said:
On March 16 we gave an indication that would reserve the underpinnings necessary for the day to day operation of supply management.
The commitment was that we would move the items about which the Hon. Member might be concerned, which are now on the tariff list, to the import control list.
It is very clear. It was very believable at that time. When they did put these on the import control list and quota for the Americans on January 1, 1989, the Americans immediately challenged the GATT. About two weeks ago their challenge was sustained by a GATT panel. The final decision has not been made yet but we know where it will likely end up; the Americans will have full access to our market. If that is not a complete misleading of Canadian dairy farmers I don't know what could be more clear.
I guess the most disconcerting part of it is that we have the Minister of Agriculture, the new minister who happens to be the Deputy Prime Minister as well, trying to rewrite history. He is saying this is all just a problem with the GATT, that it was not a problem with the free trade deal. Well, what was the former minister, Mr. Wise, talking about when he made a commitment, with an election coming up, that putting these items on the import control list would preserve them.
Now we have the Minister of Agriculture saying this is not a free trade problem, this is a GATT problem. What poppycock. Here you have two countries in a free trade zone, one with a total ban on all our products going into the United States, and when the Canadian Government put these items on the import control list immediately the Americans challenged it. Clearly there was no understanding, no arrangement under the free trade deal. The former minister totally misled the dairy farmers. The new minister is trying to rewrite history saying: "Oh well, there is no problem with the free trade". If there is no problem with the free trade deal, why is it that what the former minister promised to do is not working. It was challenged by the Americans at the GATT. That is right, it was challenged by the Americans. If you had a deal with the Americans under the free trade agreement, how come they challenged it at the GATT? Because you did not have a deal, that is the problem. We have got the worst possible precedent coming at the worst possible time because some time this
September 28, 1989

winter we are going to negotiate the new arrangements under Article 11 of the GATT as to how it will protect supply-management.
The Americans have a panel decision to open the market totally for ice cream and yogurt and a whole list of other dairy commodities. They can take that into those negotiations to destroy the whole supply-management system, which is what they have been trying to do for years so they would have total access to our markets. This has just put the whole dairy industry into complete torment as to whether or not supply-management systems for the feather and poultry industry can be maintained in this country. Clearly, we are the only country in the world that I know of that uses Article 11 of the GATT to use import controls to maintain the supply-management system. So the whole system is in serious jeopardy.
Farm quotas dropped in price by 50 per cent earlier this year with some banking institutions. The value of quotas is in jeopardy. The farm mortgages on supply-management farms are in jeopardy. The whole income support system and the whole livelihood of literally tens of thousands of farmers in this country are in jeopardy because of this action and because the government did not have in place a proper mechanism to control imports under the free trade deal with the United States.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Belsher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to assure the hon. member for Algoma that this government remains committed to supply-management as an important part of Canadian agriculture policy. The hon. member has suggested that the recent GATT panel ruling on Canadian import controls for ice cream and yogurt represents a failure on our part to protect Canadian supply-managed producers.
I would like to remind him that it was at the request of dairy producers that we added these products to the import control list under GATT Article 11 in January 1988. To quote the dairy farmers of Canada, they wrote in November 1987: "It is imperative that the Minister for International Trade take action, without further delay, to amend the import control list-to include those products for which coverage is currently not provided".
Adjournment Debate
Article 11 is designed to allow countries to regulate imports in support of national supply management programs. Canada is a member of the GATT. We have to obey the rules, and that includes using the import control list.
The U.S., which is the largest exporter of ice cream and yogurt to Canada, complained that this action did not meet all the requirements of Article 11. The U.S. pursued this complaint under the GATT dispute settlement system. The GATT panel ruled that Canadian import measures on these products were not fully consistent with our obligations under GATT
Let us also be clear about something else. The ruling was limited to two specific products. The panel's findings have no direct implications for the chicken, turkey and egg sectors which also have supply-management systems in place. We firmly believe that our supply-management programs conform with the regulations under GATT.
With regard to the GATT panel ruling, we are working closely with the dairy industry to develop a response to the panel report. We do not intend to make any immediate changes to our dairy policy.
The GATT ruling illustrates just how important it is for us to clarify the definition and the use of Article 11 during the current round of multilateral trade talks in Geneva. The panel ruling is based on rules that were negotiated in 1947. Results of the current multilateral trade negotiations will determine the rules which will govern trade into the 21st century.
As the hon. member has pointed out, the U.S. does not allow our ice cream and yogurt access to its market, and he is right in calling it unfair. We agree that it is unfair. That is why we are actively pursuing international trade reform. We want to see fair and equitable trading rules that apply to everybody in the international marketplace.
The hon. member should keep in mind that the president of Dairy Farmers of Canada stated in a press release issued on September 22, 1989: "Following our consultation with the Minister of Agriculture and officials of External Affairs, we are confident that the Canadian Government will vigorously defend the interest of supply-management in dealing with this issue as well as within the current GATT negotiations".

September 28, 1989
Adjournment Debate
TRANSPORTATION-VIA RAIL SERVICES/GOVERNMENT POSITION.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity during the adjournment debate to explain why I am dissatisfied with the government's answer to my question on VIA Rail in June of this year. I am as dissatisfied with the answers then as I am with the answers today and yesterday and the day before. Clearly this government has an extremely shortsighted view of Canada and its transportation system.
I would like to start my brief comments by quoting from a letter that was published in one of the Toronto papers. It was written by a Michael Coo of Toronto. It starts by saying:
Transport Minister Benoit Bouchard, while expressing his horror at the cost of VIA Rail to the Canadian taxpayer, went on to give his vision of Canada's transportation future-one populated with private automobiles and airplanes. I have two comments.
Bouchard says that $500 million is too much to spend (notice that the Conservatives never refer to this money as an investment) on a transportation service that is used by only 6 per cent of the Canadian travelling public. He claims that airlines, cars and bus companies all recover more of their costs than do the trains of VIA Rail. Our transport minister can only make this claim because some serious social costs are not factored into this deceptively simple equation.
He goes on to say:
There's the cost to the Canadian taxpayer, for example, of the 6,000 people who die in traffic accidents each year; and the 60,000 others who are injured. Imagine the equation if these costs were included. And that is strictly economic. It does not cover the emotional trauma of the friends and relatives of the victims.
Let me deal with that for a moment. We have a number of modes of travel in this country. Rail is the safest method of moving people from place to place. It is the most efficient in terms of fossil fuels. It could be made more efficient by electrification of the lines which would also reduce the impact on the environment and increase the speed. While the most environmental friendly method of moving people and goods is marine transport, in terms of land transportation, rail is the most environment friendly.
The next most environmental friendly mode is air travel. It only creates four times the amount of pollution as trains do in Canada. These are Canadian figures done by the Department of Transport.
The transportation mode with the most negative impact on the environment is automobiles. They contribute 17 times more carbon dioxide to the atmosphere in Canada than all of rail travel, both passenger and freight.
When this writer talks about an investment, and he talks about it in the context of an investment in safety, we also have to talk about it in the context of the investment in the future of this country and this planet in terms of minimizing our abuse of the planet we live on. Rail travel is a key element. So when we talk about the cost to the taxpayer, it is cheaper for us to provide a subsidy for a rail passenger service than it is for us to spend billions upon billions of dollars to promote road travel through the construction of ever larger highways, with more ribbons of concrete and asphalt from coast to coast. We have to keep that in mind when we talk about the cost.
That is not to say that we have to accept what VIA is doing and I, for one, do not. VIA was saddled with a situation, in reality, that was designed to fail.
I am sure the hon. parliamentary secretary will agree with me when I say that the reason his government has the ability to do what it intends to do about VIA Rail is because of the lack of legislative framework and the lack of investment by the previous government.
The Minister of Transport talked today about the billion dollars that has been poured into VIA Rail over the last number of years. I agree with him, a lot of it has been wasted because we have been repairing junk. We have been trying to keep junk on the rails, as opposed to what this government promised it would do in 1984 when it got elected. It did part of it. It restored some of the routes that the Liberals had cut. Now the government is going to cut them again. It bought new locomotives. Unfortunately, the new locomotives have to be hitched on to old locomotives which can provide the heating and the power for the junk that is being hauled behind them. What the government did not do was to buy the new rolling stock.
The former Minister of Transport, the Hon. Don Mazankowski, worked with VIA. VIA worked with the Transconsortium. Bombardier and UTDC CanCar came up with a design and a price. The government said no, it was too expensive. Transconsortium came back to the government and said, "Okay, we understand you have money problems. We will finance this operation. We will finance the construction of new equipment for VIA Rail and lease it to you". What did the government do? It said

no. This is the privatization government. It had an offer that it should not have refused but it did.
I realize my time is very tight. Let me conclude by saying that my party is not going to stop until we convince the government that what it is doing about VIA Rail is wrong. It is wrong environmentally. It is wrong socially. It is wrong economically because the cost of shutting down VIA Rail will cost more than what is going to be saved by reducing the subsidy levels.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Belsher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 3 of this year VIA Rail Canada was given new reference levels and was asked to submit to the government a new business plan which would respect new budget realities. This business plan was submitted, as requested, on June 30, 1989, and is currently under consideration. An announcement will be made in due course.
I would remind the hon. member opposite that Canadians are currently faced with a national debt which costs us $90 million a day. The subsidy paid to VIA Rail has
Adjournment Debate
increased steadily. It now exceeds $600 million yearly. Indeed, in 1988 alone this subsidy cost taxpayers $1.5 million a day, or $100 per passenger.
We simply can no longer afford this drain on the public purse, particularly since ridership has decreased by 20 per cent since 1981. In fact, rail passenger services currently retain only 3 per cent of the total Canadian intercity passenger traffic.
With 84 per cent of Canadians travelling by automobiles, and goodness knows Canadians have a love affair with the automobile, I believe that the message is loud and clear. We can no longer afford a service which is costing more and more and being used less and less.
